rationaleUpdates.text: The risk increased during September, with haze continuing to disrupt education and transport despite a decline in fire activity. By 9 September, more than 250,000 pupils across 1,030 schools in Palembang, South Sumatra, had shifted to remote learning, while around 12,800 schools were closed across Sumatra and Borneo. Over 1.4 million students were learning online across affected areas of Indonesia. Since 11 September, haze has reduced visibility in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, to below 1km, disrupting flights for several days and hampering firefighting operations. Although high-confidence fire hotspots declined significantly in Central and West Kalimantan by 14 September, and none were recorded in Riau, fires continued in parts of Kalimantan. Smoke transported from other provinces has also sustained haze in affected areas. Continued fires and cross-provincial smoke are likely to prolong exposure to hazardous air pollution, disrupt transport and education, and constrain firefighting efforts. ([AP 09/09/2026](https://apnews.com/article/indonesia-forest-fires-south-sumatra-haze-16095c9a33ff1653f74a3445645c8b8a), [AP 14/09/2026](https://apnews.com/article/indonesia-forest-fires-haze-borneo-flights-kalimantan-bb64405033429c1de557bb8f0cf6a5f9), [Reuters 23/09/2026](https://www.reuters.com/investigates/special-report/asia-weather-indonesia-wildfire-women/))

The risk continues to deteriorate based on data up to 18 July 2026. US strikes have damaged the Bunji desalination plant west of Jask in Hormozgan governorate, southern Iran, destroying the seawater intake pump and electrical transformer and disrupting the facility's operations. According to the Hormozgan Water and Wastewater Company, the damage has cut water supplies to at least 20 villages with a combined population of approximately 10,000 people. Continued insecurity and further attacks are likely to delay repair works, prolonging disruptions to safe water access. Prolonged water shortages are likely to increase reliance on unsafe water sources, heightening the risk of waterborne diseases, such as acute diarrhoea and cholera, while reducing water available for drinking, cooking, and hygiene. The disruption is also likely to increase household spending on water trucking, further straining coping capacities. ([Al Sharq 18/07/2026](https://asharq.com/sub-live/iran/60056/%D8%A5%D9%8A%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%82%D8%B7%D8%A7%D8%B9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%87-%D8%B9%D9%86-20-%D9%82%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A8%D8%B9%D8%AF-%D9%87%D8%AC%D9%88%D9%85-%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%B1%D9%83%D9%8A-%D8%A3%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%A8-%D9%85%D8%AD%D8%B7%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%AC%D9%86%D9%88%D8%A8-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AF/), [Al Arabiya 19/07/2026](https://www.facebook.com/AlArabiya/videos/%D8%A8%D8%B9%D8%AF-%D8%AA%D8%B9%D8%B1%D8%B6-%D9%85%D8%AD%D8%B7%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B6%D8%AE-%D9%84%D9%82%D8%B5%D9%81-%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%B1%D9%83%D9%8A-%D8%A5%D9%8A%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%AA%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%82%D8%B7%D8%A7%D8%B9-%D8%A5%D9%85%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%87-%D8%B9%D9%86-%D9%86%D8%AD%D9%88-30-%D9%82%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A9-/1183291447330539/))

Iran’s water scarcity situation deteriorated further in May–June 2026 amid persistent drought, depleted reserves, and growing pressure on urban water supplies and agriculture. On 3 May, authorities reported that the five dams supplying Tehran were only 18% full, with reservoir levels remaining significantly below historical averages despite some rainfall during the 2025–2026 water year. On 11 May, Iranian officials estimated that around 35 million people were experiencing water shortages across several provinces, including Tehran, Isfahan, Yazd, Qom, Alborz, and Qazvin. Authorities intensified water conservation measures and warned that rainfall remained approximately 35% below the long-term average. In June, concerns increased that conflict-related damage to infrastructure and electricity disruptions could worsen water shortages and affect irrigation systems, with agricultural representatives warning of potential crop production losses of 25–30%. The crisis is increasing risks to livelihoods, agricultural production, food security, and social stability, particularly in drought-affected areas. ([Iran Intl 11/05/2026](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605111643), [Iran Intl 03/05/2026](https://www.iranintl.com/en/202605035394), [Iran Wire 15/05/2026](https://iranwire.com/en/features/152433-tehran-faces-harsh-summer-as-irans-water-crisis-deepens/), [AJ 09/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/6/9/irans-lakes-are-vanishing-satellite-images-show-a-deepening-water-crisis-2), [NY Post 28/05/2026](https://nypost.com/2026/05/28/world-news/iranians-warned-to-conserve-water-amid-ongoing-sanctions/))

World Resources Institute ranks Iran as the 14th most water-stressed country, with 26 of 31 provinces under extreme stress. Water supply is projected to fall by 11% by 2080, while demand could rise 30% by 2050, deepening long-term scarcity. The crisis has accelerated sharply due to conflict, prolonged drought, and decades of mismanagement, pushing water systems toward collapse, particularly in Tehran and other major cities. Recent strikes have exposed the vulnerability of water and energy infrastructure, with reports of pollution affecting urban water channels. However, due to information gaps amid ongoing conflict, obtaining accurate, real-time assessments of water conditions remains challenging. ([NSB 02/04/2026]( https://www.newsecuritybeat.org/2026/04/complicating-long-term-stability-water-security-and-the-iran-war/), [Fanack Water 16/03/2026]( https://water.fanack.com/iran-war-water-crisis/), [WRI 20/03/2026]( https://www.wri.org/insights/iran-war-water-crisis-middle-east))

Iran’s water crisis has continued to deteriorate, with little meaningful recovery despite isolated rainfall events earlier in the season. While some precipitation has occurred, it has not significantly replenished reservoirs or groundwater, and inflows remain below normal. Water availability in major urban centres – including Tehran – continues to face severe stress, with authorities confirming concerns about potential rationing in 2026 as storage levels remain far below historical averages.
The situation is worsened by the conflict and heightened regional insecurity, which have strained governance capacity, disrupted infrastructure maintenance, and diverted public resources away from long-term water management. In conflict-affected and strategically sensitive areas, the risk of damage to water systems and energy supply networks has increased, while emergency preparedness and repair response times have slowed.
Overall, until March 2026, Iran stood to face critical water shortages, weak hydrological recovery, and an elevated risk of supply disruptions in the coming months. ([WRI 20/03/2026](https://www.wri.org/insights/iran-war-water-crisis-middle-east), [Resilience 05/03/2026](https://www.resilience.org/stories/2026-03-05/water-and-security-in-the-middle-east-lessons-from-the-iranian-crisis/), [Iran Focus 23/02/2026](https://iranfocus.com/economy/57198-rainfall-in-iran-has-been-higher-than-last-year-but-64-of-dam-reservoirs-are-still-empty/), [Atlantic Council 18/03/2026](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/attacks-on-desalination-plants-in-the-iran-war-forecast-a-dark-future/), [AJ 30/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/30/schools-water-industry-what-civilian-targets-have-us-israel-iran-hit))

As of February 2026, Iran’s water crisis remains severe, despite some reports of slightly higher rainfall this season. Recent data show that around 64 % of the country’s dam reservoirs are still effectively empty, reflecting persistently low inflows and prolonged drought conditions across major basins. In Tehran and surrounding regions, water resources continue to be under acute stress: key dams that supply the capital, such as the Amir Kabir and Karaj Reservoirs, remain critically low, with storage far below historical averages and still insufficient to meet urban demand if drought persists. Officials in Alborz and Hormozgan provinces have warned that decreased rainfall and lower reservoir levels could lead to water rationing and shortages later in 2026, affecting both household supplies and agricultural use. Overall, limited seasonal rainfall so far has provided only marginal relief, and Iran continues to face serious risks to water security, public health, sanitation, and livelihoods as drought conditions endure. ([Iran Focus 23/02/2026](https://iranfocus.com/economy/57198-rainfall-in-iran-has-been-higher-than-last-year-but-64-of-dam-reservoirs-are-still-empty/), [Geopolitical Monitor 12/02/2026](https://www.geopoliticalmonitor.com/irans-water-crisis-a-national-security-imperative/), [The conversation 02/02/2026](https://theconversation.com/drastic-water-shortages-and-air-pollution-are-fuelling-irans-protests-274554)

In January 2026, Iran’s water crisis remained acute and continued to worsen, following extremely limited rainfall in December 2025. Reservoir levels in Tehran and across several regions have declined sharply owing to prolonged drought and record-low precipitation. Key reservoirs, including the Amir Kabir Dam, remain near critically low capacity, severely constraining the supply of drinking water to Tehran’s population of more than ten million. Although sporadic winter rainfall in December offered marginal relief, it has been insufficient to reverse declining storage levels, leaving the risk of prolonged water shortages high. The continued drought and depleted water infrastructure continue to undermine public health, sanitation, and livelihoods, particularly in urban centres reliant on piped water systems. Water scarcity has also emerged as a key grievance during recent mass protests and is expected to further intensify social tensions in the coming months. ([CNN 01/12/2025](https://edition.cnn.com/2025/12/01/climate/iran-water-crisis-evacuate-tehran), [AJ 01/01/2026](https://studies.aljazeera.net/en/analyses/tehran%E2%80%99s-%E2%80%9Cday-zero%E2%80%9D-threat-or-opportunity-revive-water-governance-and-adaptive-water), [UNDRR 04/12/2025](https://www.preventionweb.net/news/irans-record-drought-and-cheap-fuel-have-sparked-air-pollution-crisis-real-causes-run-much), [The Guardian 15/01/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jan/15/how-day-zero-water-shortages-in-iran-are-fuelling-protests), [Euro News 15/01/2025](https://www.euronews.com/green/2026/01/15/water-shortages-blackouts-and-air-pollution-how-environmental-damage-fuelled-irans-protest))

The water crisis has intensified over the past month and worsened further in the last week. Rainfall remains roughly 85% below average in many basins, several major reservoirs have plunged to single-digit capacities, and officials report more dams at critical lows than in prior months. Reservoir levels have fallen below 3% in Mashhad and many other dam systems, government announcements include rotating cuts and partial rationing for Tehran, and satellite imagery shows rapidly shrinking river flows and exposed riverbeds. Some officials have discussed water bankruptcy and even temporary relocation or emergency measures for urban areas.
Climate-driven drought and long-term mismanagement (the overdrilling of wells, water-intensive cropping, and the proliferation of dams) continue to shrink surface and groundwater stocks in the country. Economic strains, sanctions, budget limits, and fuel/energy pressures reduce authorities’ ability to fund emergency water-trucking or large-scale infrastructure fixes. Political choices, such as continuing subsidised, water-hungry agricultural policies, remain an aggravating factor.
Because of this crisis, worsening public health risks (e.g. reduced drinking water quality and higher disease risk) are expected, along with acute impacts on food security from failed crops and livestock losses, job and income losses for rural households, and increased urban stress from rationing and possible mass migration from the hardest-hit provinces. Strained municipal services and competition for scarce water raise the risk of local unrest and increased protection needs. ([Reuters 12/11/2025](https://www.reuters.com/sustainability/land-use-biodiversity/tehran-taps-run-dry-water-crisis-deepens-across-iran-2025-11-12/), [The Guardian 09/11/2025](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/nov/09/water-levels-below-3-percent-in-dam-reservoirs-for-iran-second-city-say-mashhad-reports), [BBC 17/11/2025](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cj4172yl0l1o), [AJ 24/11/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/11/24/tehran-shrouded-in-thick-smog-as-iran-burns-dirty-fuel-amid-energy-crisis), [ABC 24/11/2025](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-11-24/iran-facing-worst-drought-in-60-years/106035210), [Iranian International 25/11/2025](https://beta.iranintl.com/en/202511250070))

The water crisis has significantly deteriorated since September 2025. Tehran faces an imminent humanitarian crisis with its main drinking water reservoir at critical depletion. By 2 November, the Amir Kabir Dam held only 14 million cubic metres of water (just 8% capacity) – sufficient for only two weeks of supply for the city's over ten million residents. This represents a catastrophic decline from 86 million cubic metres one year prior, driven by a 100% drop in precipitation. Nationally, the crisis has intensified dramatically. 19 major dams across Iran are near total depletion, with three already reaching zero capacity. Hydroelectric generation remains severely compromised, perpetuating electricity shortages alongside water rationing. At the same time, the fall rainfall (November–December) is predicted to remain below normal through early December, with precipitation delays suggesting a continuation of the water crisis. ([Essydo 03/11/2025](https://essydo.com/2025/11/03/tehran-water-crisis-only-two-weeks-of-supply/), [Daily Sabah 02/11/2025](https://www.dailysabah.com/world/mid-east/tehrans-main-reservoir-has-only-2-weeks-of-water-left-official), [Circle of Blue 04/11/2025](https://www.circleofblue.org/newsletter/the-stream-november-4-2025-tehran-two-weeks-away-from-day-zero-scenario-sees-largest-dam-at-8-percent-capacity/), [Iran HRM 13/10/2025](https://iran-hrm.com/2025/10/13/environmental-and-human-rights-crisis-in-iran-under-the-mullahs-regime/))

During May, risk levels have slightly improved because the Strait of Hormuz disruption has renewed efforts to restore Iraq's northern oil export corridor through Türkiye, which could modestly enhance export diversification and reduce some of the country's vulnerability to future maritime disruptions, although significant structural risks remain. The Strait of Hormuz disruptions have highlighted Iraq’s continued vulnerability to regional disruptions while exposing the limitations of its current oil export infrastructure. Although efforts to restore the Ceyhan pipeline could modestly reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and improve export resilience, the route is unlikely to offset major disruptions to southern exports. The situation has also increased Baghdad’s reliance on cooperation with the Kurdistan regional government, potentially strengthening Erbil’s political leverage amid disputes over revenue sharing and governance. The crisis may shift some risks from economic exposure towards heightened political tensions between Baghdad, Erbil, and Iran-aligned actors, while leaving Iraq broadly vulnerable to further regional escalation. ([CNBC 09/06/2026](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/09/iraq-uae-hormuz-oil-pipelines-oil-iran-war.html), [ISPI 21/05/2026](https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/caught-in-the-middle-iraq-amid-the-us-iran-power-struggle-238263), [Chatham House 10/06/2026](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/06/can-iraqs-new-prime-minister-finally-rein-its-armed-factions))

The risk for Iraq continues to be stable, as the ceasefire agreed from 7–8 April 2026 between Iran and the US did not effectively improve the flow of goods through the Strait of Hormoz but did restore relative security. Reports indicate that in April, Iraq’s oil exports had collapsed by up to 80% following disruptions to tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, reducing production to around 1.2 to 1.3 million barrels per day. Humanitarian implications include reduced public spending capacity, service delivery disruptions, and a potential deterioration in livelihoods. ([Oil Price 21/04/2026](https://oilprice.com/Energy/Energy-General/Iraq-Turns-to-Risky-Overland-Routes-as-Oil-Exports-Collapse.html))

The risk has deteriorated, with Iranian-backed armed groups intensifying attacks against US and Israeli assets since 1 March 2026. In response, US and Israeli forces are striking their positions in central and southern Iraq, while Iran is targeting Kurdish groups in the north, turning Iraq into a battleground of attacks and counterattacks. Prior to the escalation, over 90% of Iraq’s oil was exported through the Strait of Hormuz. The rest was exported through the Ceyhan pipeline, connected to Türkiye via Iraq’s autonomous Kurdish region, which has been closed as a safety measure in response to the conflict. With storage facilities mostly full and production halts being announced, an Iraqi government adviser has warned that suspending exports would cause losses of USD 6–7 billion per month, threatening the Government’s total income, which comprised 93% oil receipts in 2025. A sustained export halt would also threaten the Public Distribution System, an expense dependent on Iraq’s oil revenues and the primary food safety net for 39 million people (84% of the population). ([ACAPS 20/03/2026](https://www.acaps.org/fileadmin/Data_Product/Main_media/20260320_ACAPS_Ripple_effects_and_scenarios_of_the_Middle_East_conflict_.pdf))

The 25 October 2025 presidential election in Côte d’Ivoire concluded with the re-election of President Alassane Ouattara for a fourth term, with 89.77% of the vote. Although the electoral context remained highly contested — particularly following the exclusion of opposition leaders Thiam and Gbagbo — the voting day was largely peaceful, with no widespread unrest.
The government had banned protests in early October and deployed 44,000 security forces across the country, leading to a tightly controlled election environment. Participation remained low in traditional opposition strongholds, especially in the south and west, where turnout fell below 35% in some areas. In contrast, northern regions showed near-unanimous support for the incumbent, with some turnout levels exceeding 95%.
Despite reports of isolated incidents — including intercommunal violence and at least ten deaths linked to the electoral process — the elections unfolded without the large-scale violence anticipated in earlier risk assessments. Opposition parties have rejected the legitimacy of the results and called for new elections, but no major mobilisations have occurred so far. ([RFI 25/10/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251025-pr%C3%A9sidentielle-en-c%C3%B4te-d-ivoire-%C3%A0-abidjan-une-journ%C3%A9e-de-vote-dans-le-calme), [DW 27/10/2025](https://www.dw.com/fr/alassane-ouattara-reelu-quatrieme-mandat-avec-89-des-voix/a-74517060), [TV5 Monde 27/10/2025](https://information.tv5monde.com/direct/presidentielle-en-cote-divoire-les-resultats-attendus-dans-la-journee-2796017), [Le Monde 27/10/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2025/10/27/en-cote-d-ivoire-le-crepuscule-du-pouvoir-d-alassane-ouattara-reelu-pour-un-quatrieme-mandat_6649860_3212.html)).

Tensions remain high ahead of the 25 October presidential election in Côte d’Ivoire. On 8 September, the Constitutional Council published the final list of approved candidates, excluding opposition leaders Tidjane Thiam and Laurent Gbagbo. Both the Democratic Party (PDCI) and the African People's Party (PPA-CI) condemned the decision and announced joint protests. On 3 October, the Government formally banned all demonstrations contesting the Council’s ruling and mobilised 44,000 security personnel nationwide. Several opposition leaders and youth activists have been arrested since June. Meanwhile, the government and judiciary have warned media outlets against the spread of hate speech and misinformation online, threatening legal action against non-compliant publishers. Despite mounting restrictions, the opposition remains mobilised and has called for further action. The electoral campaign officially opens on 10 October. ([Le Monde 03/10/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2025/10/03/presidentielle-ivoirienne-du-25-octobre-le-gouvernement-interdit-les-manifestations-contre-l-exclusion-de-candidats-d-opposition_6644248_3212.html), [RFI 03/10/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251003-pr%C3%A9sidentielle-ivoirienne-les-manifestations-contre-l-exclusion-de-candidats-de-l-opposition-interdites), [Le Monde 19/09/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2025/09/19/presidentielle-en-cote-d-ivoire-laurent-gbagbo-ineligible-exclut-de-soutenir-un-autre-candidat_6641822_3212.html), [RFI 27/09/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20250927-c%C3%B4te-d-ivoire-les-m%C3%A9dias-appel%C3%A9s-%C3%A0-la-vigilance-quant-aux-contenus-haineux-avant-la-pr%C3%A9sidentielle)).

The political situation in Côte d’Ivoire remains tense following President Alassane Ouattara’s confirmation in late July 2025 that he will run for a fourth term. His decision has been strongly contested by the opposition, particularly the Democratic Party of Ivory Coast - African Democratic Rally and African People's Party - Côte d'Ivoire, whose leaders Tidjane Thiam and Laurent Gbagbo remain barred from the electoral roll. Despite their ineligibility, both parties submitted candidacies for Thiam and Gbagbo before the 26 August deadline, further escalating tensions. Internal divisions emerged, as alternative opposition figures attempted to enter the race and were subsequently expelled from their parties. Protests organised by the Front Commun on 9 August drew thousands, signalling popular resistance to perceived democratic backsliding. At the same time, the Independent Electoral Commission received over 50 candidacies, though only a fraction is expected to be validated by the Constitutional Council. Civil society responders warn of rising repression, including arrests of opposition youth leaders, and growing public disillusionment, especially among the country’s youth. The lack of dialogue between the ruling party and opposition continues to undermine confidence in the electoral process. ([RFI 27/08/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20250827-pr%C3%A9sidentielle-en-c%C3%B4te-d-ivoire-plus-de-50-dossiers-ont-%C3%A9t%C3%A9-d%C3%A9pos%C3%A9s-%C3%A0-la-commission-%C3%A9lectorale-ind%C3%A9pendante), [DW 30/07/2025](https://www.dw.com/fr/alassane-ouattara-est-candidat-%C3%A0-sa-r%C3%A9%C3%A9lection/a-73460127), [DW 01/08/2025](https://www.dw.com/fr/guerres-succession-partis-politiques-ivoiriens/a-73502509), [JA 09/08/2025](https://www.jeuneafrique.com/1713187/politique/en-cote-divoire-pro-thiam-et-pro-gbagbo-manifestent-contre-un-4e-mandat-de-ouattara/))

rationaleUpdates.text: Since June 2025, over 9,300 South Sudanese refugees have returned from Kakuma and Kalobeyei camps in Kenya, with daily arrivals peaking at over 220 in August. The movement is prompted by food ration cuts that have left 85,000 (45% of camp populations) without assistance, triggering protests. Kakuma and Kalobeyei were hosting nearly 191,000 South Sudanese refugees prior to the new arrivals. Two-thirds of the returnees are children, many arriving through Nadapal town into eastern Equatoria before moving to Budi, Ikotos, Kapoeta, and Torit towns. Families face ambush risks, lack of reception facilities, unsafe sanitation, and exposure to gender-based violence and disease at the border. While many returnees rejoin relatives, host households are increasingly overstretched, leading to overcrowding, food insecurity, and limited health and shelter access. Urgent needs include food, safe water, health services, and protection support especially for children and women, alongside assistance for host communities. ([UNHCR 11/09/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/south-sudan/emergency-update-returns-kenya-south-sudan), [TRT Afrika 29/08/2025](https://www.trtafrika.com/english/article/7d3492517a31), [Radio Tamazuj 14/08/2025](https://www.radiotamazuj.org/en/news/article/over-350-refugees-arrive-torit-following-food-cuts-in-kenyan-camp#:~:text=Over%20350%20refugees%20arrive%20Torit,in%20Kenyan%20camp%20%2D%20Radio%20Tamazuj))

Worsening socioeconomic conditions heightened by funding shortfalls are fuelling a rise in crime, heightening tensions between refugee and host communities, and triggering renewed protests over limited access to essential services. On 28 June 2025, a protest in Kalobeyei settlement turned violent following clashes between refugees and police. Across all camps, malnutrition is increasing, especially among children, pregnant or lactating women, and individuals with chronic illnesses, as a result of severe reductions in food rations. Gender-based violence, including intimate partner violence and early or forced marriage, remains widespread as a result of economic hardship, entrenched social norms, and overcrowded living conditions. In Kakuma and Kalobeyei, water shortages and service interruptions have led to internal relocations, disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations. Access to protection, shelter, and education remains inadequate, with girls at heightened risk of early marriage and boys pushed into informal labour. At the same time, dengue fever outbreaks in Ifo and Dagahaley camps in Dadaab have been linked to poor waste management, rising temperatures, and constrained healthcare access. ([ECHO 29/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/kenya/kenya-humanitarian-situation-refugee-camps-dg-echo-drc-echo-daily-flash-29-july-2025), [Radio Ergo 22/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/kenya/job-losses-and-aid-cuts-leave-dadaab-refugees-uncertain-their-future))

El Niño has driven a dry spell that has cut Kenya's harvest and is now expected to bring above-average short rains and flooding, with Lamu county projected to reach Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Dadaab camp Emergency (IPC Phase 4) between October–January. The dry spell caused a poor long rains harvest, with maize production estimated at 22–28% below the five-year average and losses of up to 43% anticipated in high potential North Rift counties including Trans Nzoia, Uasin Gishu, and Nakuru. The Ministry of Agriculture has acknowledged widespread crop failure in the North Rift, which produces over 60% of Kenya's maize. Wholesale maize prices in Nairobi are expected to remain 9–19% above the five-year average until January 2027, limiting food access for poor households. The October–December rains are expected to improve pastoral conditions, but in Dadaab flooding is likely to last for weeks, limiting humanitarian access and increasing waterborne disease. IPC 3 outcomes are expected to persist in Garissa, Mandera, Tana River, Wajir, and Turkana counties through January, where flooding is likely to damage transport infrastructure and displace households. A national assessment has identified 18 counties and 5,660 health facilities in areas at risk of flooding. ([FEWS NET accessed 29/09/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/kenya/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026), [FEWS NET 11/09/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/seasonal-monitor/september-2026), [The EastAfrican 15/08/2026](https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/sustainability/climate/east-africa-braces-for-prolonged-food-crisis-5558506), [Milling Middle East & Africa 13/08/2026](https://millingmea.com/kenya-anticipates-maize-deficit-of-nearly-486000-tonnes-by-late-september/), [WHO 28/09/2026](https://afro.who.int/countries/kenya/news/kenya-readies-its-military-medical-team-protect-communities-ahead-el-nino-rains))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has greatly deteriorated. On 2 March 2026, the November 2024 ceasefire collapsed, triggering a re-escalation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah that has displaced nearly 1.2 million as of 19 March. Israeli ground operations in southern Lebanon began on 16 March. The Lebanese Government has banned Hezbollah's military activities, deepening sectarian tensions among Shia communities who bear the greatest displacement burden. Civil war is unlikely, but large-scale displacement and social tensions between the IDPs and the host community are actively materialising. According to the Tension Monitoring System, anti-IDP rhetoric is increasing following continued military strikes affecting “safe areas”. ([TMS 13/03/2026](https://admin.tms-lebanon.com/StaticFiles/Files/TMS_Tensions_Pulse_-_13_March_2026.pdf), [OCHA 21/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-flash-update-10-escalation-hostilities-lebanon-19-march-2026), [AJ 02/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/2/lebanese-pm-nawaf-salam-announces-ban-on-hezbollah-military-activities)).

The risk continues to be stable overall but with a slight intensification regarding Israeli military air strikes. Between 20–21 February 2026, Israeli forces conducted multiple air strikes and drone operations across Lebanon, targeting densely populated civilian areas and Hezbollah-affiliated sites. Strikes hit the Ein Al Hilweh Palestinian refugee camp in Sidon city, killing at least ten civilians and six Hezbollah combatants, including senior commanders, and injuring 24 other civilians, including children. The attack also killed a residential building in Bekaa Valley, causing civilian casualties. The escalation raised the national threat level to ‘high’, increasing regional tensions. There are no reports of displacement, but needs for shelter and healthcare assistance are recorded. ([SARI Global 23/02/2026](https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/048e81f0-4f39-47ce-9ac6-0ff113a00a60/downloads/ea552e93-d668-4176-ba37-890c86bc6137/Bekaa%20Airstrikes%20and%20Regional%20Tension%20Dynamics.pdf?ver=1771682578376))

In January 2026, the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) completed the first phase of a U.S-backed plan to disarm Hezbollah and other groups south of the Litani River. While this has cleared some weapons from the border, Hezbollah warns that expanding the disarmament further north could trigger civil conflict as they refuse to disarm elsewhere. With increasing US and Israeli threats to attack Iran, the situation is becoming more volatile, and a renewed escalation of clashes between Hezbollah and Israel is likely, with Hezbollah being perceived as a proxy of Iran and already stating that it will not remain neutral if Iran is attacked, at the same time that Israel continues to consider Hezbollah a major threat to its national security. [(AJ 08/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/8/lebanons-mission-to-complete-disarmament-plan-of-hezbollah#:~:text=dismantle%20Hezbollah's%20weapons.%E2%80%9D-,Litani%20River,Secretary%2DGeneral%20Naim%20Qassem%20said), [Geopolitical Monitor 07/11/2025](https://www.geopoliticalmonitor.com/israeli-hezbollah-strikes-toward-a-new-conflict/), [FDD 27/01/2026](https://www.fdd.org/analysis/2026/01/27/hezbollah-we-will-not-remain-neutral-if-islamic-republic-endangered/), [TV7 27/01/2026](https://www.tv7israelnews.com/vod/series/18738/?episode-id=RTr7v66vvD4))

Lebanon is at a crossroads as Israel has set a deadline for disarming Hezbollah on 31 December, threatening renewed military action if Lebanon fails. The Lebanese Government is facing two difficult choices: attempt to forcibly disarm Hezbollah, potentially triggering internal conflict/civil war, or to fail to do so, increasing the likelihood of renewed war with Israel. The Lebanese State lacks the political and military capacity to impose disarmament on Hezbollah, which remains influential among Shia communities, despite having been significantly weakened by Israeli strikes and leadership assassinations in 2024 and 2025. Foreign pressure from the US to disarm Hezbollah continues alongside Israeli air strikes mainly targeting southern Lebanon. That said, some analysts suggest that this ultimatum is being used as political pressure rather than an imminent invasion, given Israel’s military fatigue and Lebanon’s inability to forcibly disarm Hezbollah without risking civil conflict. ([The Conversation 09/12/2025](https://theconversation.com/with-a-deadline-looming-lebanon-is-under-pressure-to-disarm-hezbollah-or-risk-another-war-271523), [SCMP 02/12/2025](https://www.scmp.com/week-asia/politics/article/3334841/israel-sets-deadline-hezbollah-disarmament-can-lebanon-deliver), [TNA 10/12/2025](https://www.newarab.com/analysis/lebanon-and-israel-will-direct-talks-change-status-quo))

Israel’s military interference in Lebanon and the disarming of Hezbollah increase the risk of rising social tensions in Lebanon. Since the ceasefire between Hezbollah and Israel on 27 November 2024, Israeli forces have continued to violate the ceasefire and kept control of five border areas. The UNIFIL also reports a concrete T-wall erected by Israeli forces in October crossing the Blue Line, rendering more than 4,000sq.m. of Lebanese territory inaccessible. On 23 November 2025, an Israeli air strike on the southern suburbs of Beirut killed Haitham Ali Al Tabtabai, Hezbollah's chief of staff, marking a serious breach of the ceasefire and possibly leading to a re-escalation of clashes between Israel and Hezbollah. On the other hand, the Lebanese army remains largely uninvolved in the Israeli attacks on Lebanon, and the Lebanese Government continues to call for the disarming of Hezbollah. This is increasing sectarian tensions, as Shia Lebanese, especially who live in southern Lebanon, feel ignored by their Government and fear being left unprotected if Hezbollah is disarmed. ([UNIFIL 14/11/2025](https://unifil.unmissions.org/unifil-statement-14-november-2025), [BBC 23/11/2025](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cn81j54xjx1o), [GIS 31/10/2025](https://www.gisreportsonline.com/r/hezbollah-disarmament-lebanon/))

In September 2025, the risk of internal tensions, protests, and displacement in Lebanon related to attempts to politically marginalise and militarily weaken Hezbollah continues to materialise and remained relevant. The situation has led to growing frustrations within Lebanon’s Shia community. The Lebanese Government aims to complete Hezbollah disarmament by the end of 2025, but Hezbollah strongly opposes this, threatening potential unrest. While a full civil war remains unlikely, localised protests, social tensions, and displacement risks persist as Hezbollah is increasingly sidelined and the needs of affected Shia communities remain unmet. ([AJ 28/09/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2025/9/28/after-war-with-israel-how-is-lebanons-hezbollah-regrouping), [ACLED 05/09/2025](https://acleddata.com/update/middle-east-overview-september-2025), [AP 06/10/2025](https://apnews.com/article/lebanon-israel-army-hezbollah-disarmament-haikal-gabriel-5e41f719da37c61517955752374fe3e5))

On 7 August 2025, Lebanon’s cabinet, led by Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, approved a US- and Gulf-backed agreement to disarm Hezbollah by the end of 2025, with the Lebanese Army due to submit an implementation plan by late August and begin phased operations immediately after. The deal includes Israeli troop withdrawals, the dismantling of Hezbollah’s missile and drone stockpiles, and an international donor conference for reconstruction. The decision sparked protests on 8 August in Beirut’s southern suburbs, where hundreds of Hezbollah supporters gathered, chanting, “Disarming will happen in your dreams,” while Hezbollah ministers walked out of the cabinet session, calling the move a “grave sin” and vowing to treat it “as if it did not exist”. Iran is likely to increase its involvement in Lebanon, as marginalising and militarily weakening Hezbollah could destabilise regional power balances.

Until July 2025, Israeli military operations against Hezbollah continued to be reported, targeting both its leadership and infrastructure, further weakening the group’s military posture. Between 14–20 July alone, Israeli forces carried out 16 air strikes, eight ground raids, and two artillery assaults across 18 Hezbollah-linked locations, killing at least 17 people, including around ten operatives. In parallel, the US has intensified diplomatic pressure to negotiate a four-month disarmament plan for Hezbollah in exchange for a full Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon. Despite these efforts, Hezbollah has refused to disarm until Israeli forces fully withdraw and halt all military operations.

Israel conducted over 50 air strikes in Lebanon in April 2025 claiming to target Hezbollah positions and infrastructure, but at least 190 deaths and 485 injuries among civilians had been recorded since the start of the ceasefire agreement on 27 November 2024.

Israel continues to violate the ceasefire agreement, with little response from the Lebanese Government. On 22 March 2025, Israel conducted air strikes in southern Lebanon in response to rockets fired towards the Israeli town of Metula. The air strikes resulted in casualties and infrastructure damage. Hezbollah has denied involvement in the rocket attacks, raising concerns about the stability of the existing ceasefire. The air strike killed at least eight Lebanese.

Foreign pressure and ceasefire conditions
Ongoing Israeli military activity
Growing frustration among the Shia population

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has deteriorated. While mass displacement from southern Lebanon had decreased from approximately 499,800 IDPs on 1 July 2026 to around 375,100 by 22 July, the nature of displacement dynamics shifted in ways that are increasing rather than reducing intercommunal pressure. Returns were driven by the inability to sustain displacement costs rather than improved conditions. Most residents who briefly returned to pilot zones in Zawtar Al Gharbiya village, Nabatiye governorate, have left again owing to extensive destruction and the absence of services, generating repeated movement between host communities and areas of origin, sustaining pressure on host areas. Host community fatigue is shifting into concrete restrictive measures, with Rmeish and Ain Ebel villages, Bint Jbeil district, South governorate, introducing registration mechanisms to monitor IDP movement, and Saida city, South governorate, identified as an emerging intercommunal hotspot. Fuel prices rising again on 25 July, with 95-octane petrol at LBP 2.414 million (USD 26.96) per 20L container, and the availability of electricity averaging only three to six hours daily are compounding economic pressure on host communities already carrying a disproportionate burden. ([IOM 02/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-displacement-tracking-matrix-mobility-snapshot-round-106-2-july-2026), [IOM 23/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/lebanon/lebanon-mobility-snapshot-round-109-23-july-2026), [Al-Sifr 08/07/2026](https://alsifr.org/displaced-lebanese), [TMS Lebanon 10/07/2026](https://tms-lebanon.com/product/report/276), [UNDP Tensions Pulse 17/07/2026](https://tms-lebanon.com/product/report/278), [Al Araby 25/07/2026](https://www.alaraby.co.uk/economy/%D8%BA%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AD%D8%B1%D9%88%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D9%8A%D8%B2%D9%8A%D8%AF-%D9%85%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%8A%D9%8A%D9%86), [Attaqa 22/07/2026](https://attaqa.net/2026/07/22/%D8%A3%D8%B2%D9%85%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%83%D9%87%D8%B1%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D9%84%D8%A8%D9%86%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%AA%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%82%D8%A8-%D8%AF%D8%B9%D9%85-%D8%AA%D8%B1%D9%83%D9%8A%D8%A7/#google_vignette))

rationaleUpdates.text: Russia continues to strengthen its presence in Libya, extending from troop and air-defence deployment in December to a full logistics and weapons hub. Advanced systems are now in play, raising the risk of an escalated proxy confrontation with Turkish-aligned forces. In June 2025, Haftar’s Libyan National Army (LNA) reportedly used advanced Russian-supplied weapons, such as Smerch rocket launchers and Tor air-defense systems, in clashes that took place in or near populated areas. This raises concern because these heavy weapons can cause significant civilian harm, and their use shows a growing Russian military role in Libya.

Russian presence continues to be reported in Libya, but it has not led to clashes between the two rival governments in Libya. On 26 May 2025, the Libyan National Army displayed a significant array of new Russian heavy weaponry for the first time during a military parade in Benghazi. Reports also indicate a sustained air bridge between Russia and eastern Libya since December 2024, including flights to Al Khadim Air Base.

Russia continues to expand its military presence in Libya, focusing on modernising the Maaten Al Sarra airbase near the Chadian and Sudanese borders. The base, developed in coordination with the Libyan National Army (LNA), is likely to serve as a logistics hub for operations in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Sudan, instead of escalating conflict in Libya. 
This shift likely reflects Russia's strategic reorientation toward the Sahel and has significant geopolitical implications, including increased regional conflict, strengthened Russian influence in Africa, and weakened Western security efforts.

rationaleUpdates.text: The political situation in Libya has been relatively calm since the brief clashes reported in September 2025. It is likely that no further escalation will occur.

While no major new offensive has erupted since the May 2025 clashes, localised incidents and militia skirmishes continue, especially near Tripoli’s southern outskirts, sustaining protection risks for civilians. Abdulhamid Al Dbeibah’s Government has sought to consolidate control, exemplified by a recent preliminary accord with the powerful Radaa Force that controls Mitiga airport, brokered through Turkish and UN mediation efforts to reduce tensions in the capital’s west. In the east and south, Saddam Haftar has intensified military deployments, notably strengthening Libyan National Army presence in Sabha and surrounding southern areas. These moves are interpreted as a strategic preparation for potential escalation, supported by continued Russian arms supplies. ([Arab News 13/09/2025](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2615212/middle-east), [The Soufan Center 08/09/2025](https://thesoufancenter.org/intelbrief-2025-september-8/), [ISPI 11/09/2025](https://www.ispionline.it/en/publication/libyas-crisis-persists-amid-tripoli-tensions-and-renewed-international-role-216835), [Agenzia Nova 02/09/2025](https://www.agenzianova.com/en/news/Libya:-Haftar's-forces-strengthen-military-presence-in-Sabha/))

Following the major clashes in May 2025, Tripoli experienced additional but more localised armed confrontations in June. On 9 June, fighting broke out between the Special Deterrence Force (SDF) and the Public Security Service, after the latter established a checkpoint in a disputed area within the zone set by the May ceasefire. The SDF responded by expanding its positions, triggering several hours of clashes. This incident indicates the fragility of the ceasefire and underlying tensions over territorial control. While no large-scale or prolonged battles were reported in July, the risk of renewed violence remains likely given unresolved rivalries and the continued presence of heavily armed factions competing for influence in Tripoli. No significant clashes were reported in July. ([Reuters 14/05/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/most-intense-fighting-years-rocks-libyan-capital-2025-05-14/), [Agenzia Nova 28/04/2025](https://www.agenzianova.com/en/news/saddam-haftar-ispeziona-le-forze-di-sicurezza-al-confine-con-lalgeria/#:~:text=The%20Chief%20of%20Staff%20of,the%20troops%20in%20border%20surveillance))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has further increased in September 2026 as forecasts indicate a strong to very strong El Niño from October 2026 to February 2027, with below-average rainfall expected across parts of southern Madagascar (Androy, Anosy, and Atsimo-Andrefana regions) during the October–November start of the rainy season. Conditions are expected to deteriorate further from October, with around 3.7 million people (11% of the analysed population) projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between October 2026 and February 2027, including nearly 426,000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). El Niño-related rainfall deficits could further reduce 2027 crop production and household incomes, particularly in the Grand South, increasing food insecurity and humanitarian needs through early 2027, though past El Niño events had limited effects on national paddy output. ([WMO 03/09/2026](https://public.wmo.int/media/news/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027), [FEWS NET accessed 05/10/2026](https://fews.net/southern-africa/madagascar/key-message-update/september-2026), [Meteo Madagascar accessed 05/10/2026](https://www.meteomadagascar.mg/prevision/previsions-saisonnieres-hiver-meteo-madagascar), [IPC 15/07/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/es/c/1165106/?iso3=MDG), [FAO 23/09/2026](https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=MDG))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk remains high and increasingly volatile. While there were indications of a partial easing in the intensity of the fuel blockade earlier in April 2026, recent large-scale coordinated attacks across multiple cities highlight a renewed deterioration in the security environment. Attacks targeting key locations, including Kati near Bamako, and the reported death of the Minister of Defence underscore the extent of armed groups’ operational reach. These developments are likely to further undermine the State’s ability to secure key transport corridors and ensure the continuity of fuel supply, which remains heavily dependent on military-escorted convoys. The reported loss of control over areas such as Kidal and the withdrawal of allied forces also point to weakening state authority in strategic regions. As a result, the risk of renewed disruptions to fuel supply and essential services remains high. Combined with continued fuel price increases and inflationary pressures, this may further constrain access to electricity, healthcare, and markets, while increasing the likelihood of social tensions. Overall, recent events suggest that earlier improvements were fragile and that the structural drivers of the risk remain firmly in place. ([RFI 27/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260427-attaques-au-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-mort-du-ministre-de-la-d%C3%A9fense-les-populations-inqui%C3%A8tes-malgr%C3%A9-un-certain-calme), [RFI 02/04/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260402-mali-autorit%C3%A9s-accusent-des-entreprises-utiliser-crise-carburant-pour-gonfler-leurs-prix), [BBC 24/04/2026](https://www.bbc.com/afrique/articles/cyv1rpn4753o), [Ledjely 01/04/2026](https://ledjely.com/2026/04/01/mali-la-hausse-du-carburant-fait-craindre-une-spirale-des-prix/), [Timbuktu Institute 17/04/2026](https://timbuktu-institute.org/index.php/toutes-l-actualites/item/1509-le-mali-entre-chocs-externes-et-defis-internes))

The risk has slightly deteriorated, with more fuel shortages reported. On 28 March 2026, the Government of Mali raised diesel prices by nearly 30% and petrol prices by 13% in response to supply disruptions by the Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin blockade. The heightened impacts of the fuel shortages increase the likelihood of civil unrest. On 25 March, diesel shortages in Bamako intensified as limited fuel imports were further redirected to support electricity generation during a heat wave. Several fuel stations ran out of diesel, leading to long queues at remaining supply points and disrupting urban mobility. At least 100 public transport vehicles were taken out of service, while construction-related transport (e.g. sand and gravel trucks) halted. ([TRT 10/03/2026](https://www.trtafrika.com/article/27f0213a3997), [Bloomberg 28/03/2026](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-28/mali-raises-petrol-diesel-prices-and-cuts-some-fuel-subsidies))

Since January, the risk linked to the fuel blockade and related insecurity has remained high and volatile, with continued attacks despite temporary supply improvements in Bamako. While fuel availability in the capital improved in early February, the broader trend points to sustained operational disruption and geographic expansion of insecurity.  Key developments include renewed large-scale JNIM attacks on fuel convoys near Kayes, leading to the killing of drivers and military escorts and prompting a nationwide transport strike on 9 February. In central Mali, state forces conducted airstrikes in Macina (Ségou Region) following reported insurgent activity in Sikasso, while in Kidal region, a convoy was targeted by both JNIM and Azawad Liberation Front elements, suggesting overlapping armed actor pressure in the north. Continued road blockades affecting multiple localities and persistent electricity shortages (6–8 hours per day in Bamako) indicate structural fragility. In the short to medium term, continued convoy insecurity and transport disruptions risk renewed fuel shortages, rising prices, reduced market access, and further constraints on electricity supply, livelihoods, and humanitarian access, particularly outside the capital. ([DW 10/02/2026](https://www.dw.com/fr/focus-sahel-plus-villes-sous-blocus-du-jnim-au-mali/a-75901357), [RFI 03/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260203-au-mali-l-approvisionnement-en-carburant-plie-mais-ne-rompt-pas), [RFI 10/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260210-mali-cibles-d-attaques-jihadistes-des-chauffeurs-routiers-appellent-%C3%A0-un-arr%C3%AAt-de-travail), [RFI 20/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260220-mali-une-frappe-de-drone-des-rebelles-du-fla-contre-l-arm%C3%A9e-fait-des-morts-des-deux-c%C3%B4t%C3%A9s)).

Since the previous update, the risk associated with the fuel blockade has remained elevated but volatile, with short-lived improvements followed by renewed disruption. While some fuel circulation has resumed intermittently, shortages persisted throughout January 2026, indicating neither clear escalation nor stabilisation. Key developments point to a broadening of the blockade’s scope. In Bamako, electricity supply remains limited to around five to seven hours per day, and fuel availability continues to be intermittent, with long queues and growing reliance on informal markets. In the southwest, Nioro du Sahel remains under a near-total blockade since early September 2025, with movement restrictions, reported abductions, and the increasing scarcity of food, medicines, fuel, and water. In parallel, attacks linked to Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin have expanded beyond fuel convoys to economic infrastructure, including mid-January 2026 attacks on industrial sites in Kayes and late January attacks on fuel convoys. Authorities have announced tighter fuel controls and reinforced escorts ahead of Ramadan, but continued incidents suggest a persistent risk of disruption to essential services, rising living costs, constrained access to markets, and increasing humanitarian needs in affected urban and blockaded areas. ([RFI 10/01/2026)[https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260110-mali-des-habitants-de-nioro-du-sahel-racontent-le-blocus-jihadiste-qui-dure-depuis-cinq-mois), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-la-fourniture-d-%C3%A9lectricit%C3%A9-et-de-carburant-reste-tr%C3%A8s-insuffisante-les-bamakois-se-r%C3%A9signent), [RFI 14/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260114-mali-le-manque-de-carburant-%C3%A0-l-a%C3%A9roport-de-bamako-perturbe-certaines-liaisons), [RFI 16/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260116-mali-blocus-jihadiste-%C3%A0-nioro-du-sahel-la-situation-est-sous-contr%C3%B4le-selon-les-autorit%C3%A9s-de-transition), [RFI 12/01/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260112-mali-comment-et-pourquoi-des-jihadistes-ont-attaqu%C3%A9-trois-sites-industriels-de-la-r%C3%A9gion-de-kayes), [RFI 02/02/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260202-au-mali-les-autorit%C3%A9s-veulent-s%C3%A9curiser-l-apprivisionnement-de-carburant-pour-le-mois-de-ramadan))

Since early December, the JNIM has resumed attacks on fuel convoys after a temporary slowdown observed in late November. The initial lull allowed some fuel deliveries to reach Bamako and Mopti, briefly reducing shortages and restoring limited electricity and public services. However, renewed ambushes in Bougouni, Ouélessébougou, and Ségou, including the destruction of over 15 fuel tankers and the killing of drivers, have reinstated supply chain disruptions and public anxiety. In Bamako, queues at petrol stations have grown again, diesel has become scarce, and intermittent power cuts have returned. While 300 trucks were received ahead of the AES summit in mid-December, the improvement remains temporary. In Mopti and surrounding areas, fuel convoys have resumed under heavy military protection, but the quantities remain insufficient to meet the demand. Electricity has returned for around nine hours per day, and some economic activity has restarted, though fuel prices on the black market remain triple the official rate.  The blockade continues to affect humanitarian operations and access to essential services. In areas such as Koulikoro, Sikasso, and Koutiala, fuel scarcity persists, with limited electricity, inaccessible health services, and rising transport costs. The JNIM’s strategy has evolved beyond physical control, aiming to delegitimise the state through economic strangulation and selective violence. The group is reportedly consolidating control over rural areas by offering basic services (such as justice and security) under Islamic governance, gradually normalising its authority. 
([Echoes of the Sahel 17/12/2025](https://mailchi.mp/9406facccf81/sahel-news-round-up-21010886?e=fe2a2db667), [RFI 17/12/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251217-mali-%C3%A0-bamako-l-approvisionnement-en-carburant-est-fluctuant), [RFI 12/12/2025](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20251212-mali-retour-du-carburant-et-du-courant-%C3%A0-mopti-une-am%C3%A9lioration-notable-mais-encore-trop-r%C3%A9duite), [Revue Conflicts 26/11/2025](https://www.revueconflits.com/jnim-au-mali-letranglement-de-bamako-et-la-strategie-du-califat-par-consentement/))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk continued to increase during the second half of September as JNIM sustained high-intensity operations in central Mali, further challenging state control and security along strategic corridors. Following its 10 September attack on the Dioura military camp, which killed more than 100 soldiers and resulted in more than 100 being captured, JNIM shelled the Sévaré air base for six consecutive nights between 14–19 September and attacked a forward operating base in Konna on 20 September. The attacks indicate JNIM's continued capacity to target major military positions and transport corridors in Mopti region, while supply routes to Bamako remain exposed to disruption by armed groups. Although no significant new joint operation by JNIM and the Azawad Liberation Front was identified after the previous update, the sustained pressure by JNIM, alongside the continued presence and coordination capacity of both groups in northern Mali, maintains the risk of further territorial and humanitarian deterioration. Continued insecurity is likely to constrain population movement, trade, and humanitarian access, particularly across central and northern Mali. ([Reuters 21/09/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/al-qaeda-linked-militants-kill-more-than-100-malian-soldiers-attack-this-month-2026-09-21/), [CT 24/09/2026](https://www.criticalthreats.org/analysis/ethiopia-tigray-tplf-fano-china-prc-djibouti-jnim-mali-sudan-saf-rsf-somalia-aussom), [AJ 22/09/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/22/mali-marks-independence-amid-a-worsening-security-crisis))

The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as continued operations of Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin and the Azawad Liberation Front sustained pressure on state control in northern and central Mali. Fighting around Kidal contributed to the displacement of nearly 40,000 people, including around 15,000 who sought refuge in Gao and Ménaka regions, increasing pressure on already-strained services. Conflict involving non-state armed groups continued to disrupt markets, livelihoods, and supply routes, worsening food insecurity. From June–August, 1.56 million people faced Crisis (CH Phase 3) or worse food insecurity, including nearly 57,000 in Emergency (Phase 4). ([Global Watch 13/08/2026](https://globalwatch.info/en_GB/articles/gc7/features/2026/08/13/feature-02/Nearly-40-000-displaced-following-Mali-fighting-surge-sources), [FAO 27/08/2026](https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=MLI&lang=en&), [DW 17/08/2026](https://amp.dw.com/fr/laide-humanitaire-aux-d%C3%A9plac%C3%A9s-internes-sorganise-%C3%A0-gao-et-menaka-mali-jnim/a-78392740)).

The risk deteriorated further in July 2026. Although Malian and African Corps forces regained Anéfis following the fighting of 4–9 July, subsequent attacks show that they have not secured the surrounding territory or key transit routes. Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Front de libération de l'Azawad (FLA) continued joint operations against military positions and convoys in northern Mali, while JNIM intensified pressure in central Mali, including by taking the Kouakourou military camp and forcing the locality’s approximately 5,000 residents to flee. These developments confirm that the JNIM–FLA operational cooperation remains active and that armed groups retain the capacity to isolate strategic locations, disrupt military resupply, and generate new displacement. Humanitarian conditions have worsened alongside the escalation. More than half of Kidal’s population has moved towards Gao, Ménaka, or Algeria, while markets are operating at reduced capacity, and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) food insecurity is expected to persist in Kidal and Ménaka. Attacks on civilians and vehicles continue to disrupt trade and movement elsewhere, while blockaded communities, such as Diafarabé, remain at risk of renewed shortages despite limited food deliveries. Humanitarian operations remain suspended in Kidal, and insecurity continues to restrict access in Gao, Mopti, and Tombouctou. Over the next one to three months, continued JNIM–FLA operations, insecurity along strategic corridors, and retaliatory military strikes are likely to generate further displacement and civilian protection risks while constraining trade and humanitarian assistance. Limited funding and access will further reduce the capacity to respond as food needs increase during the lean season. ([FEWS NET 06/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-mise-jour-des-messages-cles-persistance-de-linsecurite-alimentaire-durgence-phase-4-de-lipc-dans-les-regions-de-kidal-et-de-menaka-juillet-2026-janvier-2027), [ACLED 20/07/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/malian-military-losing-against-jnim), [RFI 22/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/podcasts/revue-de-presse-afrique/20260722-%C3%A0-la-une-au-mali-mbareck-ag-akli-figure-clef-de-la-r%C3%A9bellion-ind%C3%A9pendantiste), [RFI 25/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260725-mali-apr%C3%A8s-la-d%C3%A9route-de-l-arm%C3%A9e-malienne-face-aux-jihadistes-du-jnim-kouakourou-s-est-vid%C3%A9-de-ses-habitants), [WFP 22/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/wfp-mali-country-brief-july-2026), [RFI 30/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260730-mali-la-ville-de-diafarab%C3%A9-enfin-ravitaill%C3%A9e-mais-en-faible-quantit%C3%A9-apr%C3%A8s-un-an-de-blocus-du-jnim)).

The risk has deteriorated further. Since 4 July 2026, Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin and the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) have launched a new wave of coordinated attacks across northern and central Mali, including Aguelhok, Anéfis, Gao, and Sévaré. Armed groups have seized Anéfis town and continue to besiege the military camp, while clashes, shelling, drone attacks, aerial strikes, and attempts to reinforce the camp continue. The attack on a military convoy travelling from Gao towards Anéfis on 9 July indicates that the armed groups are sustaining pressure on strategic routes and military positions in Kidal region. The escalation confirms that coordinated JNIM–FLA operations remain active and are likely to further disrupt movement along key routes linking Gao, Kidal, and other northern areas. This increases risks of civilian exposure to armed violence, movement restrictions, new displacement, and humanitarian access constraints in areas already facing severe needs. Around 683,000 people live in the affected towns and surrounding regions, including approximately 363,000 already in need of humanitarian assistance. The deterioration comes amid persistent blockade-related impacts. Tombouctou has faced severe fuel shortages, disrupting electricity and water services, while there are reports of serious abuses by all conflict parties since the April escalation, including civilian killings, vehicle burnings, and abusive counter-insurgency operations. ([RFI 09/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260709-mali-le-convoi-militaire-en-route-vers-an%C3%A9fis-attaqu%C3%A9-par-le-fla-et-le-jnim-pr%C3%A8s-de-tabankort), [RFI 06/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260706-mali-l-arm%C3%A9e-et-l-africa-corps-russe-tiennent-le-camp-d-anefis-assi%C3%A9g%C3%A9-et-bombard%C3%A9), [RFI 04/07/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260704-mali-des-localit%C3%A9s-dans-le-nord-et-une-prison-dans-le-sud-vis%C3%A9es-par-des-attaques), [France 24 29/06/2026](https://www.france24.com/en/africa/20260629-all-warring-parties-in-mali-committed-grave-abuses-against-civilians-report-says))

The risk remains active. While some local agreements have eased movement restrictions in specific areas, recent developments indicate that coordinated JNIM–FLA operations continue to generate significant humanitarian consequences through displacement, access constraints, market disruptions, and the progressive isolation of northern and central regions. The humanitarian impact of the April escalation remains evident in Kidal and neighbouring regions. Food security conditions in Kidal are expected to deteriorate from Crisis (IPC Phase 3) to Emergency (IPC Phase 4) from June onwards as insecurity, military bombardments, reduced trade flows from Algeria, and the absence of escorted convoys further isolate the region during the lean season. Access to humanitarian assistance remains severely constrained, while worsening market shortages, high prices, and restrictions on livestock movements are reducing household access to food and income.
Displacement and service disruptions continue to increase humanitarian needs. WFP reported 2,328 newly displaced people from Kidal to Gao following the April crisis, while all 16 schools in Kidal remained closed through May, disrupting education for more than 2,900 students. At the same time, insecurity continues to affect key transport corridors and access to essential goods. Although a locally negotiated agreement led JNIM to lift its nearly two-year blockade of the road linking Bamako to Nara and Mourdiah, other areas remain affected by movement restrictions, insecurity, and fuel shortages. In Tombouctou, prolonged fuel shortages linked to JNIM's blockade have contributed to disruptions in electricity and water services, forcing residents to rely on limited alternative water sources. Similar disruptions to trade flows and fuel supplies continue to affect purchasing power and access to basic goods across northern and central Mali.
Over the next one to three months, continued JNIM–FLA pressure on transport corridors, urban supply chains, and contested territories is likely to sustain displacement, restrict humanitarian access, and worsen food insecurity, particularly in Kidal, Ménaka, Gao, and parts of Mopti and Tombouctou. While local agreements may temporarily reduce violence in some areas, they do not address the broader deterioration in state control, humanitarian access, and civilian protection conditions across northern and central Mali.
([FEWS NET 11/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-key-message-update-food-insecurity-deteriorates-emergency-ipc-phase-4-kidal-amid-severe-conflict-may-september-2026), [WFP 18/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/wfp-mali-country-brief-june-2026), [Education Cluster 24/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mali/mali-compte-rendu-reunion-mensuelle-du-mois-de-juin-2026-meeting-minutes), [RFI 26/06/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260626-mali-tombouctou-priv%C3%A9e-d-%C3%A9lectricit%C3%A9-et-d-eau-depuis-quatre-jours-de-carburant-depuis-un-mois), [RFI 25/06/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260625-au-mali-le-blocus-jihadiste-lev%C3%A9-sur-la-route-menant-%C3%A0-mourdiah-et-nara)).

The risk of flooding and weather-induced displacement in Mozambique has intensified since December 2025 as La Niña–driven rainfall has translated into sustained, on-the-ground impacts. During January 2026, above-average rainfall persisted across central and northern provinces, with repeated heavy rain episodes falling on already saturated catchments. This has driven further rises in the Zambezi, Licungo, Pungue and Save rivers and expanded flooding in Zambézia, Sofala, Tete, Manica and Nampula.
Cyclonic disturbances and active low-pressure systems in the Mozambique Channel have acted as key aggravating factors, generating short-duration but high-intensity rainfall that has overwhelmed drainage systems and weakened flood defences. Localised infrastructure damage, crop losses and continued population displacement indicate an escalation from forecast risk to realised impact.
In the short to medium term, continued flooding through the remainder of the rainy season is likely to deepen humanitarian needs, disrupt access to affected communities, increase food insecurity due to crop destruction, and strain basic services, particularly in low-lying river basins and coastal districts.
([ECHO 29/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-severe-weather-and-floods-update-ingd-noaa-cpc-echo-daily-flash-29-january-2026), [ECHO 20/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-severe-weather-and-floods-update-ingd-copernicus-emsr-dg-echo-noaa-southern-africa-echo-daily-flash-20-january-2026), [UNFPA 19/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/unfpa-mozambique-heavy-rains-and-flooding-flash-update-19-january-2026), [IOM 19/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/mozambique-heavy-rains-and-flooding-displacement-update-18-january-2026), [OCHA 18/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/mozambique/flash-update-no3-heavy-rains-and-floods-central-and-southern-mozambique-18-january-2026))

The risk has further increased in September 2026 as forecasts indicate a strong to very strong El Niño from October 2026 to February 2027, with below-average rainfall expected across parts of southern Madagascar (Androy, Anosy, and Atsimo-Andrefana regions) during the October–November start of the rainy season. Assessments indicate that the lean season has already started earlier than usual in the Grand South, with poor households exhausting food stocks in September following below-average 2025/26 harvests and increasingly relying on markets and negative coping strategies. Conditions are expected to deteriorate further from October, with around 3.7 million people (11% of the analysed population) projected to face Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse between October 2026 and February 2027, including nearly 426,000 in Emergency (IPC Phase 4). El Niño-related rainfall deficits could further reduce 2027 crop production and household incomes, particularly in the Grand South, increasing food insecurity and humanitarian needs through early 2027, though past El Niño events had limited effects on national paddy output. ([WMO 03/09/2026](https://public.wmo.int/media/news/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027), [INGD 21/09/2026](https://ingd.gov.mz/comunicado-especial-no-03-ingd-cenoe-2026-2027-de-21-de-setembro-de-2026), [WMO 01/10/2026](https://wmo.int/media/news/el-nino-will-unleash-multiple-hazards-south-west-indian-ocean-region), [IPC 09/09/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165444/?iso3=MOZ))

The risk has worsened since July 2026 as forecasts indicate increasing confidence that a strong El Niño will persist through the 2026–2027 rainy season, raising the likelihood of drought in southern and central Mozambique and flooding in northern provinces. Humanitarian organisations and government stakeholders have intensified preparedness efforts, with anticipatory action triggers already activated in several districts owing to the heightened climate risk. Conflict-related displacement in Cabo Delgado province and funding shortfalls for humanitarian operations further compound existing vulnerabilities. In the short to medium term, affected households may face reduced agricultural production, declining food access, displacement, disease outbreaks, and increased needs across the food security, nutrition, health, and WASH sectors. ([FAO 29/07/2026](https://www.fao.org/mozambique/news/details/mozambique-strengthens-anticipatory-action-ahead-of-a-record-el-ni%C3%B1o-with-support-from-fao-and-wfp/en), [UN News 30/07/2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/07/1168056), [FEWS NET 07/2026](https://fews.net/southern-africa/mozambique/key-message-update/july-2026)).

rationaleUpdates.text:
Since the December 2025 elections in Myanmar, conflict and protection risks have not decreased but instead remain acute. The elections were widely criticised as neither free nor fair. Association of Southeast Asian Nations declined to endorse or observe the polls, citing the exclusion of major opposition parties and the inability to conduct voting in conflict-affected areas. The United Nations and international rights groups also raised concerns over intimidation, arrests, and coercive practices ahead of the vote, while over 300 civil society organisations urged the international community to reject the process as a military entrenchment exercise. In contrast, countries such as China and India maintained engagement, reflecting geopolitical divisions over recognition.

Post-election dynamics have reinforced humanitarian risks. Continued aerial bombardments in Rakhine and Sagaing have caused civilian casualties and disrupted essential services. UNICEF has warned that children are increasingly affected, while the World Food Programme has cautioned that funding gaps and access constraints could worsen hunger and malnutrition in 2026. Ongoing conflict, displacement, and restricted humanitarian access indicate that the elections have not contributed to de-escalation, and civilian protection risks remain high nationwide.

The risk of escalating armed conflict ahead of Myanmar’s elections on 28 December has intensified since October. Political repression has deepened, with over 30,000 opponents detained since 2021 and new laws criminalising dissent. Military offensives and air strikes have surged in Magway, Mandalay, and Sagaing, killing civilians and destroying infrastructure, while opposition forces have vowed to block polling stations. Indicators of escalation include reinstated compulsory military service, expanded drone warfare, and coercive measures forcing civilians to return to insecure areas to vote. Humanitarian conditions have deteriorated sharply; displacement has risen beyond 3.6 million, food insecurity has worsened, and aid access has collapsed. Short- to medium-term impacts include heightened civilian casualties, mass displacement, and the severe disruption of relief operations, particularly in contested regions where violence and intimidation tactics are expected to intensify.
([HRW 16/11/2025](https://www.hrw.org/news/2025/11/16/myanmar-elections-a-fraudulent-claim-for-credibility), [GI 28/11/2025](https://www.globalissues.org/news/2025/11/28/41769), [OCHA 17/11/2025](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/myanmar/ocha-myanmar-humanitarian-update-no50-17-november-2025), [FR 19/11/2025](https://www.fortifyrights.org/mya-inv-2025-11-19/), [MoeMaKa Media 30/10/2025](https://moemaka.net/eng/2025/10/myanmar-military-news-updates-oct-30-2025-morning/), [VOH 18/11/2025](https://www.visionofhumanity.org/election-plans-amid-myanmars-humanitarian-crisis-and-ongoing-conflict/))

The risk increased in September as military operations expanded across Launglon, Long Lone, Thayetchaung, and Yebyu townships and along Highway 8. In late September, troops advanced into Thit Taw Taung in Yebyu and Kyauk Sin in Launglon. Operations in Long Lone between 8–10 September killed four civilians and displaced nearly 5,000 people. In Yebyu, increased troop deployments, checkpoints, and questioning restricted civilians’ access to plantations and workplaces, while reports of civilians being forced to guide troops or act as human shields indicate heightened protection risks. Since late September, flooding and landslides have compounded these impacts by damaging roads and communications. Continued military activity has constrained displacement and evacuation, while blocked roads and limited access to machinery have delayed humanitarian assistance to villages isolated by floodwater and landslides. The combination of conflict and natural hazards is likely to increase displacement, restrict access to livelihoods and essential services, and prolong humanitarian access constraints. ([HURFOM 11/09/2026](https://rehmonnya.org/four-civilians-including-a-man-over-90-reported-killed-during-junta-operation-in-long-lone), [HURFOM 22/09/2026](https://rehmonnya.org/villagers-reported-used-as-human-shields-as-junta-tightens-movement-restrictions-in-yebyu), [HURFOM 02/10/2026](https://rehmonnya.org/military-advances-force-villagers-to-flee-amid-flooding-and-landslides-in-yebyu-and-launglon), [UCA News 02/10/2026](https://www.ucanews.com/amp/floods-kill-41-in-myanmars-tanintharyi-region/115595), [Sentinel Asia accessed 03/10/2026](https://sentinel-asia.org/EO/2026/article20261001MM.html))

The risk increased during September as armed groups are expanding and consolidating overlapping areas of operation. Armed group activity continued to place pressure on Nigerien forces in western Niger during the second half of September, although no significant direct clashes between the Support Group for Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP) were reported. On 26 September, two attacks attributed to Islamic State militants targeted Nigerien security forces near Abala in Tillabéri region and at Dabagu in Konni department, Tahoua region, killing 50–57 soldiers and gendarmes. The simultaneous attacks across two regions indicate ISSP's continued capacity to conduct high-impact operations against state forces beyond its core areas in Tillabéri. Violence also continued in Dosso region, with attacks reported in Dioundiou department during the second half of September, reinforcing indications of the southward expansion of armed group activity. While these developments increase pressure on security forces and confirm the continued geographic expansion of armed groups, there is not yet clear evidence of an escalation in direct JNIM–ISSP confrontation in Niger. ([Le Monde 25/09/2026](https://www.lemonde.fr/afrique/article/2026/09/25/au-niger-l-organisation-etat-islamique-de-plus-en-plus-puissante_6782594_3212.html), [E News 25/09/2026](https://enews.com.ng/2026/09/57-niger-security-personnel-reportedly-dead-in-seperate-attacks/), [Naija News 25/09/2026](https://newsnaija.com.ng/35-reportedly-dead-as-violence-hits-niger-in-three-separate-incidents/))

The risk has deteriorated as sustained operations of Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and Islamic State – Sahel Province (ISSP) across western Niger in August 2026 further weakened the State’s ability to maintain security in rural areas and increased civilian exposure to violence, displacement, and movement restrictions. Attacks across Diffa, Dosso, Maradi, and Tillabéri regions between 21–25 August, including JNIM’s seizure of a military post in Bangoume commune, Tillabéri, and an ISSP assault on a gendarmerie post in Tessa commune, Dosso, that killed at least 18 gendarmes, indicate a widening operational footprint beyond established hotspots. The coup attempt on 29 August, linked partly to military discontent over mounting casualties, further raises concerns over the security forces’ capacity to contain armed-group activity. In Tillabéri, where more than 330,000 people are displaced, insecurity is contributing to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity through January 2027, with Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes projected among the most asset-depleted displaced households. ([Critical Threats 03/09/2026](https://www.criticalthreats.org/analysis/niger-coup-russia-algeria-sudan-rsf-chad-ethiopia-drc-m23-fardc), [Niger Report 08/08/2026](https://nigerreport.net/security-challenges-persist-in-nigers-tillaberi-region-after-latest-attack/), [METIS 24/08/2026](https://metis.fenixinsight.com/event/679840), [FEWS NET accessed 13/09/2026](https://fews.net/west-africa/niger)).

Western Niger has become the main area of competition between Jama'at Nasr Al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) and the Islamic State in the Sahel Province (ISSP) as both groups intensify operations to expand and consolidate territorial influence. In June 2026, ISSP launched large-scale attacks against military positions in Inates and Banibangou, while JNIM expanded its presence through coordinated attacks targeting Niamey Airport and several localities along the Niger–Burkina Faso border. Although direct confrontations between the groups remain limited, their competition is contributing to more frequent and higher-intensity attacks against military positions and strategic infrastructure, further destabilising Tillabéri region. Continued insecurity is driving displacement, disrupting livelihoods and markets, and restricting humanitarian access. By mid-July, around 230,000 people had been newly displaced since the beginning of 2026, while Crisis (IPC Phase 3) food insecurity is expected to persist across conflict-affected areas of Tillabéri until at least January 2027. Attacks near Tera in July indicate that the operational tempo remains high, suggesting western Niger will remain the centre of JNIM–ISSP competition in the coming months. ([ACLED 06/07/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/africa-overview-july-2026), [ACLED 19/06/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/what-does-niamey-airport-attack-mean-nigers-security), [WFP 20/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/niger/wfp-niger-country-brief-july-2026), [FEWS NET 30/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/niger/niger-food-security-outlook-persistent-conflict-maintaining-crisis-ipc-phase-3-tillabery-diffa-and-tahoua-june-2026-january-2027), [UNICER 03/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/niger/unicef-niger-humanitarian-situation-report-no-1-mid-year-january-june-2026)
