rationaleUpdates.text: Risk levels have increased as Netanyahu publicly announced on 28 May that he directed the IDF to take control of 70% of the Gaza Strip, far beyond the roughly 53% allotted under the October 2025 ceasefire deal with Hamas. At the beginning of June, Israel already controlled 60% of the Strip. Renewed Israeli military escalation in Gaza has led to rising civilian casualties and widespread displacement, with evacuation and shelter-in-place orders issued in multiple areas, including Gaza City, Deir Al Balah, Maghazi, Bureij, and Nuseirat. Between January–April 2026, malnutrition admissions increased by 21% compared to the same period in 2025 despite the ceasefire, indicating worsening food insecurity. By mid-May, World Central Kitchen, previously distributing around 1 million meals daily, reduced operations by 50% because of rising operational costs linked to the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruptions, affecting at least 13,000 displaced people across 12 camps in Khan Younis. ([WCK 14/05/2026](https://wck.org/news/wck-to-return-gaza-operations-to-pre-ceasefire-levels-amid-funding-challenges/), [Times of Israel 28/05/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-says-he-told-idf-to-seize-70-of-gaza-strip-well-beyond-terms-of-truce/), [UNRWA 26/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/unrwa-situation-report-223-humanitarian-crisis-gaza-strip-and-west-bank-including-east-jerusalem-enar))

The situation has deteriorated because Gaza faces further food access disruptions with the production of bread, a primary food source, dropping by 50% in late April given restricted aid deliveries, flour shortages, and a lack of fuel for running bakeries. Humanitarian access restrictions have increased since early March following the escalation in the Middle East involving Israeli and US attacks on Iran, resulting in decreased inflows into the Strip – currently at around 260 tonnes per day against a required 450 tonnes, equivalent to only 38% of pre-October 2023 levels. The bread bundles that international organisations can produce cover only 30% of needs. Food insecurity projections for mid-April suggest that 1.6 million may be facing Crisis (IPC Phase 3) or worse levels, likely worsening as restrictions on the entry of aid, including flour, persist. There are already reports of people queuing for hours for bread only to return without it. ([TNA 28/04/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/gazas-bread-crisis-deepens-50-production-cuts), [IPC 19/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/gaza-strip-ipc-acute-food-insecurity-and-acute-malnutrition-special-snapshot-october-2025-april-2026-published-19-december-2025), [WFP 23/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/wfp-palestine-emergency-response-external-situation-report-87-23-april-2026-reporting-period-1-14-april-2026))

Although the conflict in the Middle East between Iran and Israel/US was not originally suggested as a trigger for this risk, it has contributed to a spike in food prices as most border crossings have been closed since 1 March 2026, except for Kerem Shalom for limited humanitarian movement and the Rafah border crossing for people’s movement only until 25 March. Aid deliveries into Gaza have dropped by around 80%, with only 590 trucks entering in the first week of March compared to 4,200 previously. The reduced flow has led to severe shortages, with flour prices tripling and tomatoes more than doubling. Many families have depleted their income sources, further challenging food access. The shortages of food and cooking equipment have suspended the operations of some community kitchens, risking the reversal of food security improvements. ([UNRWA 05/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/unrwa-situation-report-211-humanitarian-crisis-gaza-strip-and-occupied-west-bank-including-east-jerusalem-enar), [AJ 10/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/3/10/gaza-food-prices-soar-as-border-closures-deepen-shortages-amid-iran-war), [TNA 19/03/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/gaza-aid-plunges-during-iran-war-israel-tightens-blockade)))

The risk has deteriorated, with Israel announcing the indefinite closure of crossings into Gaza, including the Rafah border crossing, on 1 March 2026 following the start of the Israel/US war on Iran on 28 February. This has immediately suspended aid flow into the strip and suspended humanitarian operations inside Gaza, including the World Central Kitchen. This will disrupt access to food and spike food prices. The food insecurity deterioration has become highly likely. ([WCK 01/03/2026](https://wck.org/news/media-alert-border-closure-forces-world-central-kitchen-to-pause-gaza-meal-operations/))

The risk continues to be stable, although the ceasefire between Hamas and Israel agreed on 10 October 2025 remains highly fragile. Between 10 October 2025 and 10 January 2026, at least 1,244 Israeli violations of the ceasefire were recorded, including incursions beyond the yellow line and control of roughly 58–60% of Gaza, particularly in Gaza city, Khan Younis, and Rafah. Humanitarian access is still heavily restricted; aid convoys, medical supplies, and winter relief have been delayed or blocked, worsening conditions for civilians, especially after flooding from Storm Byron in December 2025 affected 55,000 families. ([TNA 15/01/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/gaza-records-over-1200-israeli-ceasefire-violations), [OCHA 18/12/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-349-gaza-strip), [AJ 22/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/politics/2026/2/22/%D9%85%D8%A7-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B0%D9%8A-%D8%AA%D8%BA%D9%8A%D8%B1-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D9%88%D8%B5%D9%88%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%AA))

The risk has significantly deteriorated. Between 20–28 July 2026, settler violence in the West Bank reached a critical inflection point, with two Palestinians killed in Deir Jarir on 20 July, followed by clashes on 24 July in Tal village near Nablus in Area B under joint security control that killed four Palestinians and two Israelis, with Israeli soldiers present but initially failing to intervene. The Palestinian death toll from settler-related incidents in 2026 had reached 18 by 19 July, already exceeding the 2025 total. Israel responded by deploying 26 military battalions, the largest West Bank deployment in years, and launching mass arrest operations across Hebron, Jenin, Nablus, Ramallah, and Tulkarem, arresting at least 80 Palestinians in 24 hours, alongside accelerated demolitions and new settlement announcements. Israeli military analysts assess that the risk of a major West Bank escalation exceeds that of renewed confrontation with Iran, warning of a potential new uprising driven by institutional impunity and the absence of any political process. [MC Doualiya 20/07/2026](https://www.mc-doualiya.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B4%D8%B1%D9%82-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%88%D8%B3%D8%B7/20260720-%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%AF-%D8%BA%D9%8A%D8%B1-%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%A8%D9%88%D9%82-%D9%84%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%AA%D9%8A%D8%B7%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B6%D9%81%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D9%88%D8%B3%D8%B7-%D8%A7%D8%AA%D8%B3%D8%A7%D8%B9-%D9%86%D8%B7%D8%A7%D9%82-%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%AA%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%A1%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%AA%D9%88%D8%B7%D9%86%D9%8A%D9%86), [HRW 27/07/2026]
(https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/west-bank-surge-settler-violence-threatens-mass-atrocities-enar), [BBC Arabic 24/07/2026](https://www.bbc.com/arabic/articles/c1l1pg54mjdo), [Al Jazeera 25/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/7/25/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B6%D9%81%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A8%D8%B9%D8%AF-%D8%AA%D9%84-%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%B9%D9%8A%D8%AF-%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A), [Sky News Arabia 25/07/2026]
(https://www.skynewsarabia.com/middle-east/1882760-%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84-%D8%AA%D8%B9%D8%AA%D9%82%D9%84-66-%D9%81%D9%84%D8%B3%D8%B7%D9%8A%D9%86%D9%8A%D8%A7-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B6%D9%81%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A9), [OCHA 23/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/opt-humanitarian-situation-report-23-july-2026), [Al-Rai 28/07/2026](https://alrai.com/article/10968832/%D8%B9%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D9%88%D8%AF%D9%88%D9%84%D9%8A/%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%B0%D9%8A%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D9%85%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%81%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%B1-%D9%88%D8%B4%D9%8A%D9%83-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B6%D9%81%D8%A9/amp)).

The risk has deteriorated during August 2026 ahead of the 27 October Israeli elections, as Israeli military control continues to consolidate across Gaza. Further westward advancement of the Yellow Line into eastern Middle Area, Gaza city, and Khan Younis, alongside Israel’s approval of the Green Rafah infrastructure project in eastern Rafah under military supervision, indicates that temporary military positions are increasingly becoming permanent areas of control. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's rejection of the US-backed 15-point road map on 8 August, with Jared Kushner subsequently confirming that implementation was contingent on full Hamas disarmament, has reduced prospects for diplomatic measures that could constrain this consolidation before the elections. The expansion is already affecting humanitarian operations, with Yellow Line advances triggering evacuation and shelter-in-place orders affecting more than ten UNRWA premises, indicating that further territorial consolidation is likely to compound existing access constraints and accelerate the deterioration of humanitarian operational capacity. ([OCHA 07/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/opt-humanitarian-situation-report-7-august-2026), [CNN 09/08/2026](https://arabic.cnn.com/middle-east/article/2026/08/09/hamas-netanyahu-trumps-plan-for-gaza), [AJ 10/08/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/amp/news/2026/8/10/%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%A4%D9%88%D9%84-%D8%A8%D9%85%D8%AC%D9%84%D8%B3-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85-%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%A9-%D8%BA%D8%B2%D8%A9-%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%85%D8%A9), [UNRWA 30/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/unrwa-situation-report-231-humanitarian-crisis-gaza-strip-and-occupied-west-bank-including-east-jerusalem-enar), [AJ 09/08/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/9/israels-green-rafah-plan-aims-to-fragment-gaza-experts-say)).

A weak La Niña pattern has persisted into early 2026, increasing the likelihood of above-normal rainfall across several parts of the Philippines during the January–March period. According to Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA), La Niña conditions are expected to enhance monsoon activity and rainfall intensity, heightening the risk of flooding, flash floods, and rain-induced landslides, particularly in low-lying, riverine, and mountainous areas. Seasonal outlooks also project multiple tropical cyclones entering or forming within the Philippine Area of Responsibility between February and mid-2026, compounding rainfall-related hazards.
Humanitarian risks remain elevated. Recurrent heavy rains and potential early-season cyclones increase the probability of agricultural damage, infrastructure disruption, and localized displacement, especially in flood-prone and typhoon-exposed provinces. The Philippines’ multi-hazard exposure means that consecutive weather events could strain local response capacity and prolong recovery in vulnerable communities. Overall, La Niña conditions are likely to sustain above average hydrometeorological risks through at least Q1 2026, with potential escalation as the cyclone season progresses.

The risk has increased as El Niño strengthens, with impacts on agriculture and water availability already reported in parts of the Philippines. A strong to very strong El Niño is expected to persist through the first half of 2027 and may peak before the end of 2026. In Davao region, 4,447 farmers have been affected, with approximately 4,791 hectares of crops damaged and PHP 444 million in losses since El Niño emerged in August. Rice production has been particularly affected. In Agusan del Sur province, low river levels, cracked rice fields, dry-spell damage to corn plantations, and critically low water supplies at the provincial government centre were reported in September. Further intensification could increase crop losses and water shortages, reducing agricultural income and access to water among farming communities. These impacts could increase food security and WASH needs over the coming months. The nationwide scale of humanitarian needs remains unclear. ([PIA 22/09/2026](https://pia.gov.ph/news/mindanao/dr/rice-farmers-urged-to-shift-to-drought-tolerant-crops-amid-el-nino), [GOVPH 15/09/2026](https://agusandelsur.gov.ph/2026/09/15/agusan-del-sur-guv-seeks-el-nino-data-for-possible-calamity-declaration/), [PAGASA accessed 30/09/2026](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/agri-weather/monthly-agroclimatic-review-and-outlook))

The risk is active and stable, as during July 2026, weak-to-moderate El Niño conditions developed in the tropical Pacific, marking the onset of the anticipated event. Updated climate projections indicate a 97% probability that El Niño would persist through the first half of 2027. These projections indicate that El Niño will intensify over the coming months, with a 57% probability of strong conditions from July–September 2026 and an 81% probability of very strong conditions from October–December 2026 and from November 2026 to January 2027. Forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of drought and below-normal rainfall in parts of the Philippines from late 2026, with potential impacts on agricultural production and water availability. Until July, however, there remained no evidence of the developing El Niño causing significant agricultural losses, widespread water shortages, food price increases, or increased humanitarian needs. ([PAGASA accessed 11/08/2026](https://bagong.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/climate/el-nino-la-nina/monitoring), [PAGASA 22/07/2026](https://www.pagasa.dost.gov.ph/index.php/climate), [The Philippine Star 27/07/2026](https://www.philstar.com/business/2026/07/27/2544851/government-scrambles-respond-looming-el-nio)).

rationaleUpdates.text: Somalia's political crisis has entered its most acute phase, further worsening the risk of large-scale violence. The Parliament's mandate expired on 14 April 2026 without elections being held, and President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud extended his own term unilaterally past the initial 15 May expiry of the mandate. Election talks between the federal government and the Somali Future Council collapsed, and Puntland and Jubaland have formally withdrawn from the federal system in protest at the new constitution, with more than 100 MPs and senators from both states boycotting the final constitutional vote. Opposition figures have begun planning protests in Mogadishu, which triggered fierce urban clashes on 3 June between government forces and opposition-aligned militias. At least 13 people were killed and 189 wounded, with civilian displacement and restricted movement reported across several districts. Turkish intelligence and Western diplomats brokered a fragile ceasefire by 5–6 June, but the underlying political impasse remains entirely unresolved. The fracture between the Government and key member states, combined with an increasingly delegitimised executive, sustains elevated risks of renewed violence and further displacement. ([Hiiraan Online 04/06/2026](https://www.hiiraan.com/news4/2026/Jun/205332/mogadishu_clashes_kill_13_injure_189_people_unbacked_report_says.aspx), [UNHCR/Protection Cluster 06/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-protection-civilians-poc-note-escalation-armed-violence-mogadishu-6-june-2026), [Al Jazeera 05/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/5/why-mogadishu-clashes-are-deepening-somalias-political-crisis-again), [Somali Guardian 06/06/2026](https://www.somaliguardian.com/news/somalia-news/somalia-somali-mogadishu-security-operation-clashes/), [Garowe Online 04/06/2026](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/turkish-intelligence-mediates-to-defuse-somalia-election-crisis))

Since March 2026, the risk has intensified as Somalia’s political transition has moved deeper into a constitutional crisis. Somali election talks between the Federal Government and the Somali Future Council collapsed in February, and tensions over contested constitutional amendments disrupted a parliamentary session in Mogadishu, highlighting a hardening political stand‑off. The Government is pressing ahead with a new constitution and a one‑person‑one‑vote road map, while key federal member states and opposition leaders denounce unilateral changes and signal possible boycotts or parallel processes. These developments increase the likelihood of legitimacy disputes, renewed confrontation between federal and regional parties, and localised violence in flashpoints such as Baidoa, Gedo, Jubaland, and Puntland. In the short to medium term, further deterioration could trigger additional conflict‑related displacement, restrict humanitarian access, and heighten needs for populations already facing high food insecurity and protection risks. ([SG 23/02/2026](https://www.somaliguardian.com/news/somalia-news/somalia-election-talks-collapse-over-constitutional-row/), [Dawan Africa 15/04/2026](https://www.dawan.africa/news/somali-future-council-threatens-separate-election-timeline), [AS 15/04/2026](https://addisstandard.com/mandate-expired-authority-retained-somalias-risky-power-extension-amid-emerging-rivalries/), [ICG accessed 07/05/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/africa/horn-africa/somalia), [Puntland Post 18/04/2026](https://puntlandpost.net/2026/04/18/jubaland-waan-is-difaacaynaa-haddii-federaalku-isku-dayo-in-uu-doorasho-ka-qabto-gedo/))

In January 2026, political risk in Somalia has stabilised despite heightened tensions surrounding electoral reforms. For the first time in decades, Somalia has moved away from its clan-based political model by holding direct local elections in Mogadishu under a one-person, one-vote system. The polls were conducted in December 2025 without major security incidents, despite threats from Al Shabaab, marking a notable improvement in election-related security management in the capital. That said, the process unfolded amid strong political opposition, with several opposition leaders criticising the reforms and key federal member states, including Puntland and Jubaland, rejecting the approach and questioning its legitimacy. While the successful conduct of the elections reduced the immediate risk of violence in Mogadishu, unresolved disputes between the Federal Government and regional authorities continue to pose medium-term risks to political cohesion and federal–state relations. ([ACSS 13/01/2026](https://africacenter.org/spotlight/en-elections-2026/somalia/), [DW 25/12/2026](https://www.dw.com/en/mogadishu-holds-election-that-could-determine-somalias-future/a-75300474),  [AJ 25/12/2025] (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/12/25/somali-capital-holds-first-direct-election-in-five-decades))

Somalia has announced plans to hold the country’s first direct universal suffrage elections in Banadir region, which includes Mogadishu, on 30 November 2025. The pilot marks a major shift away from Somalia’s traditional clan-based, indirect electoral system towards a one-person, one-vote model. Nearly one million people have registered to vote, with youth aged 18–34 representing the majority at about 69%. By October, 14 political associations had been cleared to participate, signalling the emergence of competitive multiparty politics at the local level. The move has sparked political tension, with key federal member states, such as Puntland and Jubaland, rejecting the plan. They argue that the Federal Government’s approach lacks national consensus, is financially unsustainable, and risks deepening political divisions. The opposition, Somalia’s National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission, has reaffirmed its commitment to proceed with preparations, including voter education, security arrangements, and logistical planning, to ensure the elections are transparent and peaceful. ([GO 25/10/2025](https://www.garoweonline.com/en/news/somalia/somalia-s-first-direct-vote-sparks-dispute-as-fgs-moves-ahead-with-election-plans))

The developing El Niño, forecast to intensify from mid-2026, raises the prospect of a significant shift in Somalia's hazard profile later in the year. El Niño is expected to be more intense than the 2023 event, with the main risk shifting from drought to flooding along the Juba and Shabelle rivers as the October–December Deyr season approaches. There is also a possibility of riverine flooding before El Niño's arrival, driven by above-normal Kiremt rains in the Ethiopian highlands between June–September. Communities already severely weakened by consecutive drought seasons – with depleted livestock, exhausted water infrastructure, and eroded coping capacity – are unlikely to have recovered before potential flooding arrives, raising the risk that a drought-to-flood transition will deepen displacement and disease burdens across southern and central Somalia.
([FAO 30/04/2026](https://www.fao.org/somalia/news/details/somalia-faces-a-triple-threat-of-drought--middle-east-conflict-and-predicted-el-ni%C3%B1o-flooding--fao-warns/en), [OCHA 06/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/somalia/somalia-2025-2026-drought-emergency-situation-report-no-5-6-april-2026), [ICPAC 19/05/2026] https://www.icpac.net/news/drier-than-usual-conditions-with-warmer-than-average-temperatures-expected-in-the-greater-horn-of-africa/))

Since March 2026, the drought risk has remained very high and its impacts have further intensified, even though the Deyr season has ended. Failed 2025 Deyr rains and an atypically harsh Jilaal have driven widespread Crisis (IPC Phase 3) and Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes, with some areas at risk of Catastrophe/Famine (IPC Phase 5), alongside increasing drought‑related displacement and livestock losses. Millions are facing severe food insecurity and water shortages, with coping capacity eroded after consecutive poor seasons. Gu 2026 forecasts point to a delayed onset and high temperature stress, with only partial and uneven rainfall recovery expected, suggesting that acute needs will remain elevated through at least mid‑2026, particularly in central and southern Somalia. ([FEWS NET 10/02/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/somalia/key-message-update/january-2026), [OCHA 09/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-2025-2026-drought-emergency-situation-report-no-4), [FAO 03/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/swalim-update-somalia-gu-2026-climate-outlook-issued-3-march-2026), [MoECC 16/02/2026](https://moecc.gov.so/somalia-releases-gu-2026-seasonal-climate-outlook-highlighting-increased-rainfall-and-flood-risks/))

Drought has intensified over the past month, driven by worsening climatic conditions and increasing humanitarian impacts. Prolonged dry conditions have affected an estimated 4.61 million people as of January, with at least 120,000 people displaced between September and December, particularly in central and Lower Somalia. Critical water infrastructure continues to fail, with over 170 boreholes and shallow wells reported non-functional, further reducing access to safe water. The drought has also disrupted basic services, forcing approximately 75,000 students to drop out of school. The January–March 2026 Jilaal dry season is expected to aggravate water scarcity, abnormal livestock movements and rising livestock mortality, likely worsening acute food insecurity. Continued displacement towards urban centres and IDP sites is expected, increasing pressure on already fragile living conditions, access to services and livelihood opportunities.([OCHA 21/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-2025-drought-emergency-situation-report-no-2-21-december-2025), [OCHA 27/01/2026] (https://reliefweb.int/report/somalia/somalia-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026))


30/10/2025
Forecast remains concerning about the dry situation in Somalia. Dry conditions driven by below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures are expected to worsen in already drought-affected northern regions, while recovery in the south following the 2025 Gu and Hagaa rains may stall owing to poor Deyr performance. There is an increased likelihood (around 55%) of drier-than-normal conditions across southern and central Somalia and coastal areas of Somaliland. A moderate likelihood (about 45%) of dry conditions is also forecast for Somaliland and central Puntland. In the northeast, conditions remain uncertain, but heat stress risks are expected to stay high. Overall, drought conditions in Somaliland and Puntland (northern Somalia) are likely to deteriorate further. ([FAO 06/10/2025](https://faoswalim.org/resources/site_files/Somalia_climate_outlook_for_the_2025_deyr_season.pdf))

The risk has intensified after President Kiir dissolved the transitional government on 22 September, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December. The decree removed all five Vice Presidents, including the suspended First Vice President Riek Machar, dissolved the national and state legislatures, and replaced ministers and governors with caretaker appointees, ending the power-sharing arrangement set up under the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of Conflict in South Sudan. It followed amendments to the National Elections Act, signed on 21 September, that allow Kiir to remain in office with full powers throughout the election period. Kiir had also dismissed the chair of the National Elections Commission on 15 September without giving a reason. The South Sudan Opposition Movements Alliance has rejected the caretaker administration as illegitimate and the elections as a sham, and warned on 28 September that the crisis could lead to further violence and insecurity across the country. The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan, which had already warned in August that elections without safeguards and inclusive dialogue could fuel renewed conflict and atrocity crimes, said the window to prevent a return to 2013–2018 levels of violence and displacement is closing. Government and Sudan People's Liberation Army-in-Opposition forces continue to fight in Jonglei and Upper Nile states, a conflict that predates the election, and no escalation directly linked to the election has been reported so far. Any such escalation during the election period would add to displacement in areas where humanitarian access is already constrained. ([AJ 23/09/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/23/south-sudan-dissolves-government-ahead-of-first-ever-national-elections), [ABC News 23/09/2026](https://abcnews.com/International/wireStory/south-sudan-president-dissolves-transitional-government-ahead-long-136675583); [Radio Tamazuj 29/09/2026](https://www.radiotamazuj.org/en/news/article/ssoma-kiir-has-usurped-authority-calls-for-new-peace-process), [UN News 20/08/2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/08/1168173), [Amnesty International 22/09/2026](https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2026/09/south-sudan-authorities-must-protect-civic-space-ahead-of-scheduled-national-elections/), [ICG accessed 29/09/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/africa/horn-africa/south-sudan))

The Government's decision to press ahead with the December 2026 elections, sidelining the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan (R-ARCSS) in the process, has sharpened the risk of a return to full-scale civil war. On 22 July, President Kiir assented to a bill bypassing R-ARCSS consensus procedures. On 7 August, the Council of Ministers approved amendments stripping out the permanent constitution and national census as preconditions for the vote, over the objections of Machar's SPLM-IO faction. Machar himself remains under house arrest, facing trial without full due process guarantees, while a USD 75,000 party registration fee and the rejection of a rival "IO Party" registration have shut his faction out of the electoral process entirely, removing any incentive for the main opposition faction to accept the outcome peacefully. The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan has warned that these conditions, compounding the fighting and displacement already in progress, risk a rushed election, triggering renewed crimes. ([CHRSS 21/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/south-sudan/brink-preventing-atrocity-crimes-and-safeguarding-south-sudans-transition-august-2026), [The EastAfrican 02/08/2026](https://www.theeastafrican.co.ke/tea/news/east-africa/south-sudan-peace-sponsors-jittery-election-5543180), [Radio Tamazuj 08/07/2026](https://www.radiotamazuj.org/en/news/article/machar-trial-adjourned-after-co-accused-miss-court-power-outage))

Risk levels remained stable during May as no major clashes were reported, but humanitarian conditions continue to worsen. In the first three months of 2026 alone, 366,000 people lost access to MSF-supported healthcare following the bombing of Lankien and the looting of facilities across Jonglei. By the end of May, there was no surgical capacity remaining in the conflict-affected areas of the state. The Government committed on 8 May to facilitate humanitarian access to Akobo, though aid organisations warn access remains severely constrained. Akobo is projected to reach Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5) food insecurity levels in April–July 2026, with over 7.8 million people nationally facing crisis-level hunger or worse. With the rainy season now underway, displaced families face growing isolation as flooding restricts humanitarian operations.
([MSF 06/03/2026](https://www.doctorswithoutborders.org/latest/south-sudanese-government-offensive-forces-mass-evacuation-akobo-and-suspension-msf), [MSF 06/05/2026](https://prezly.msf.org.uk/no-accountability-one-year-after-old-fangak-hospital-bombing-warring-parties-must-spare-last-remaining-hospitals-jonglei-south-sudan), [UNHCR 05/06/2026](https://www.unhcr.org/news/briefing-notes/renewed-insecurity-and-rising-displacement-south-sudan-s-jonglei-put-thousands), [OWP 08/05/2026](https://theowp.org/south-sudan-commits-to-humanitarian-access-in-akobo-as-catastrophic-hunger-looms/), [DRC 28/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/south-sudan/drc-situational-report-5-jonglei-emergency-28-may-2026))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) expanded their territorial control in Blue Nile. On 11 August, the alliance captured Geisan, followed by Al Kurmuk on 13 August, after the Sudanese Armed Forces withdrew from the town. The offensive triggered significant displacement; more than 5,000 people had reached Ed Damazine by 18 August, while IOM reported nearly 14,000 displaced from Geisan and Al Kurmuk throughout the month. By 28 August, RSF and SPLM-N had claimed control of Bakori and Surkum military bases, while satellite analysis identified around 100 additional light technical vehicles at an Ethiopian base near Assosa, indicating preparations for further advances towards Ed Damazine. ([Critical Threats 20/08/2026](https://www.criticalthreats.org/analysis/sudan-rsf-splm-issp-lakirawa-nigeria-africa-file-august-20-2026), [AJ 13/08/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/13/sudan-army-says-rsf-advance-on-key-town-bordering-ethiopia], [Sudan Tribune 18/08/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/317605), [Radio Tamazuj 25/08/2026](https://www.radiotamazuj.org/en/news/article/blue-nile-civil-society-warns-of-deepening-crisis-as-thousands-flee-fighting), [Radio Dabanga 30/08/2026](https://www.dabangasudan.org/en/all-news/article/yale-researchers-warn-of-major-military-build-up-at-ethiopian-base-near-sudan-border)).

The risk escalated in July 2026; conflict and displacement pressures in Blue Nile remained active, with Ed Damazine increasingly absorbing people displaced by months of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the alliance between the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudan People's Liberation Movement–North (SPLM–N). On 23 July, a reported SAF drone strike hit a gathering of displaced people in Ed Damazine, killing several and underscoring the growing exposure of displaced populations in the state capital. In late July, community-based civil society responders warned of worsening humanitarian and health conditions among thousands of IDPs in Ed Damazine and surrounding areas, with heavy rains further aggravating conditions in camps and informal settlements. While there is still no clear evidence that the RSF/SPLM-N alliance has advanced decisively into Ed Damazine, the combination of continued clashes, displacement towards the city, drone incidents, and deteriorating camp conditions suggests the risk pathway is moving closer to materialisation. ([Sudan Tribune 24/07/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/316532#google_vignette), [Sudan Tribune 28/07/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/316760), [UK Home Office 23/07/2026](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/sudan-country-policy-and-information-notes/country-policy-and-information-note-security-situation-sudan-july-2026-accessible))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as attacks by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) intensified around Al Obeid city, North Kordofan state. On 12 August, suspected RSF drones struck the city, killing two people and injuring others. From 14–15 August, RSF attacks on Um Arda locality, Tamid village, and Al Khor Al Abyad village, North Kordofan state, displaced 4,250 people; the attack on Um Arda alone killed 18 civilians and displaced more than 300 families towards Al Obeid. On 20 August, RSF attacks on Um Dareisa village and Al Shaqla village, North Kordofan state, killed six civilians and displaced more than 1,000 people towards Al Obeid city. These attacks increased pressure on the city and advanced the siege and displacement pathways of the risk. ([Reuters 12/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/rsf-renews-assault-sudans-al-obeid-drones-strike-capital-witnesses-say-2026-08-12/), [Sudan Tribune 15/08/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/317416), [AA 16/08/2026](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/insecurity-displaces-over-4-000-people-in-sudans-north-kordofan-in-2-days-un-migration-agency-says/4028830), [Sudan Tribune 20/08/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/317681)).

The risk escalated in July as pressure from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on Al Obeid intensified into siege-like conditions, with repeated drone attacks, worsening shortages, and growing protection concerns. UN reporting describes Al Obeid as a key civilian, administrative, and humanitarian hub where RSF drone attacks and insecurity along exit routes have increased, while attacks have affected power stations, fuel depots, water facilities, transport routes, hospitals, markets, schools, and residential areas. Drone strikes have worsened water and fuel shortages in the city, while women and girls face the dual risk of daytime drone attacks and sexual violence when fetching water at night. Displacement pressure has also increased in Kordofan, with displacement sharply rising as the conflict escalated. Although widescale movement towards White Nile has not fully materialised, the siege and displacement pathway advanced significantly in July. ([UN 03/07/2026](https://www.unognewsroom.org/teleprompter/en/3184/hrc-62-urgent-debate-3-july-2026), [IOM 03/07/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/displacement-rising-crisis-escalates-kordofan-sudan), [MSF 15/07/2026](https://www.doctorswithoutborders.org/latest/sudan-drone-attacks-are-worsening-water-and-fuel-crisis-el-obeid), [Reuters 24/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/women-sudans-al-obeid-face-drone-attacks-rape-when-fetching-water-un-says-2026-07-24/))

triggers.title: RSF encirclement of Al Obeid

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as restrictions on trade routes and markets increasingly constrained food availability and affordability in West Kordofan. On 6 August, Northern state authorities tightened controls on commercial trucks travelling towards Kordofan and Darfur, confiscating two trucks carrying food and fuel; millet reached SSP 900,000 per sack and onions SSP 2 million in An Nuhud locality, West Kordofan. By 15 August, households were consuming ambaz, an animal-feed byproduct, amid unaffordable food prices. On 26 August, authorities of the Rapid Support Forces closed public markets, restricted movement, and shut down Starlink services in An Nuhud, further disrupting commercial activity and food access. Although Khartoum state had reopened the export route on 14 August, continued restrictions elsewhere compounded market disruption. ([Darfur24 26/08/2026](https://darfur24.com/en/2026/08/06/northern-state-tightens-ban-on-goods-bound-for-kordofan], [Darfur24 15/08/2026](https://darfur24.com/en/2026/08/15/west-kordofan-families-turn-to-animal-feed-as-food-prices-soar/), [Sudan Tribune 26/08/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/317893), [The Citizen 14/08/2026](https://citizen-sd.com/2026/08/khartoum-government-lifts-ban-and-reopens-export-route-to-trucks/)).

The risk remained stable in July 2026, although there is limited reporting on new or expanded state-level bans on goods specifically affecting West Kordofan. The broader trigger pathway, however, remained concerning as conflict, access constraints, and rising costs continued to threaten food security and market functioning across the country. By mid-July, Sudan could slide further into hunger because of conflict, aid cuts, and rising agricultural costs, including higher diesel and fertiliser prices linked to wider regional disruption. Food insecurity continues to be reported, with Famine (IPC Phase 5) conditions under a worst-case scenario linked to intensified conflict and further restrictions on humanitarian access and the movement of goods and people. For West Kordofan, this means the risk has not clearly escalated through a new trade-ban development, but the underlying market and food security drivers remain highly fragile and could deteriorate quickly. ([WFP/FAO/UNICEF 15/05/2026](https://www.wfp.org/news/joint-news-release-wfpfaounicef-risk-famine-persists-nearly-195-million-people-face-acute-food), [IPC 15/05/2026](https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1163315/), [Reuters 14/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/sudan-risks-deeper-hunger-crisis-due-war-aid-cuts-hormuz-disruption-says-wfp-2026-07-14/))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk remained stable during July 2026, with no clear public reporting of open clashes between SAF and its allied armed groups in Khartoum. The underlying drivers of the risk remained present. External pressure on SAF to distance itself from armed groups with political Islamist leanings continued in the background, following the earlier designation and sanctions targeting the Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade. The brigade continued to play an important role in SAF-aligned mobilisation, with links to Islamist networks and alleged ties to Iranian support, sustaining the potential for friction between SAF's military dependence on allied groups and external pressure to contain them. At the same time, developments in July centred more on drone strikes, the escalation in Kordofan, and RSF external support networks than on fragmentation among SAF-aligned groups in Khartoum. The risk therefore remains active but has not clearly moved closer to materialisation during July. ([Henry Jackson Society 19/06/2026](https://henryjacksonsociety.org/2026/06/19/the-safs-islamist-shadow-the-al-baraa-bin-malik-brigade-and-sudans-escalating-war/), [UK Home Office 23/07/2026](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/sudan-country-policy-and-information-notes/country-policy-and-information-note-security-situation-sudan-july-2026-accessible), [Reuters 29/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/boeings-identified-reuters-report-carried-weapons-sudanese-paramilitary-un-2026-07-29/))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) resumed long-range drone attacks across areas held by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), increasing the threat to infrastructure supporting eastern supply routes. On 12 August, suspected RSF drones targeted Ad Damar, Al Obeid, Atbara, Bahri, and Um Durman; SAF air defences intercepted several drones, but others struck a mosque and an electricity transformer in Bahri and targets in Al Obeid, killing two people. On 18 August, SAF reported intercepting two RSF FH-95 drones near Jargeira and Bara, while further attacks were reported around Bara, Gebrat Al Sheikh, and the export route towards Al Obeid. The widening geographic reach and repeated attacks indicate an increased likelihood of disruption to transport and supply flows, although Port Sudan itself was not struck. ([AA 12/08/2026](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/africa/rsf-drone-attacks-target-5-sudanese-cities-military-intercepts-drones/4024820), [Reuters 12/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/rsf-renews-assault-sudans-al-obeid-drones-strike-capital-witnesses-say-2026-08-12/), [Dabanga 18/08/2026](https://www.dabangasudan.org/en/all-news/article/saf-shoots-down-two-rsf-long-range-drones-in-north-kordofan)).

The risk remained stable in July, with no clear public reporting of renewed large-scale drone attacks on Port Sudan or sustained disruptions to the eastern supply corridor during the month. Concerns persisted that external supply networks could continue to provide the Rapid Support Forces with weapons, drones, and personnel, potentially sustaining or expanding its long-range strike capabilities. At the same time, the wider Red Sea environment became more sensitive during the month, with regional maritime security concerns increasing amid attacks and threats affecting shipping routes near the Red Sea and Suez-linked corridors. ([Reuters 29/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/boeings-identified-reuters-report-carried-weapons-sudanese-paramilitary-un-2026-07-29/), [Reuters 30/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/us-military-says-it-hit-dozens-irans-irgc-targets-2026-07-30/), [Financial Times 31/07/2026](https://www.ft.com/content/926bad8a-55e0-4d1d-8612-7ebd0aaef4ee))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk deteriorated in August 2026 as damage to the Merowe power system caused widespread and prolonged electricity disruptions across areas under the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces. In early August, a fire at the Merowe Dam power station damaged transmission lines, leaving Khartoum, Northern, Red Sea, and River Nile states without stable electricity for nearly two weeks. Electricity was restored to Khartoum, Red Sea, and River Nile states on 16 August after repairs to damaged cables and a key transformer substation. Repeated drone attacks have also targeted Merowe infrastructure since the start of the conflict. Although the cause of the August fire was not established, the prolonged outage demonstrated the vulnerability of the Merowe-linked power system and its wider impact on essential services. ([Sudan Tribune 17/08/2026](https://sudantribune.com/article/317524), [Arab News 06/08/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/middle-east/merowe-dam-outage-brings-sudans-power-crisis-back-into-focus-2653663), [Reuters 28/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/extensive-power-cuts-hamper-life-sudan-2026-08-28/)).

The risk escalated in July 2026 following renewed drone activity against power infrastructure in northern Sudan. On 16 July, drones from the Rapid Support Forces targeted a power station in the north, triggering a fire and injuring a security guard. The attack highlights the continued vulnerability of electricity infrastructure, as previous strikes on power facilities linked to the Merowe grid have caused widespread blackouts across Northern state, disrupting water pumping, health services, irrigation, and other essential public services. While there was no clear indication of structural damage to the Merowe Dam itself within the month, the renewed targeting of northern power infrastructure shows that the trigger pathway remains active. ([Anadolu Agency 16/07/2026](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/africa/rsf-drone-strike-targets-power-station-in-northern-sudan/3999702), [TRT World accessed 03/08/2026](https://www.trtworld.com/article/6e5c66dcb19e), [Reuters 18/01/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/blackouts-hit-wide-swathes-army-controlled-sudan-after-drone-attacks-2025-01-18/)

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk remained stable in July 2026, with continued pressure on Sudanese refugees and returnees in Chad, although there was no clear evidence of a sudden mass return movement into West Darfur during the month. By 30 June, more than 1.33 million people had crossed into Chad since the start of the Sudan crisis, including over 405,000 Chadian returnees, with further arrivals expected as conflict and food insecurity persist in Darfur. At the same time, severe funding shortfalls continued to reduce access to food, water, shelter, protection, and healthcare for refugees in Chad, weakening coping capacities in refugee-hosting areas. ([IOM 30/06/2026](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/chad-sudan-crisis-response-situation-update-66-june-2026), [UNHCR/WFP 09/04/2026](https://www.unhcr.org/africa/news/press-releases/funding-shortfalls-put-lifelines-risk-sudanese-refugees-chad), [IOM 08/06/2026](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/dtm-sudan-cross-border-monitoring-report-4))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk remains stable with no major events indicating an escalation or a de-escalation. The war in the Middle East that started on 28 February 2026 between the US/Israel and Iran has exposed deep fragmentation within Syria’s Alawite community, with competing positions ranging from alignment with Iran, to neutrality and external protection, to a shift towards rights-based political representation. This reflects a broader transition away from a unified ideological alignment towards survival-driven strategies shaped by fear, uncertainty, and the absence of a central leadership. ([An-Nahar 27/03/2026](https://www.annahar.com/arab-world/arabian-levant/292964/3-%D9%85%D9%82%D8%A7%D8%B1%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D9%83%D9%8A%D9%81-%D9%8A%D8%AA%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%88%D9%8A%D9%88%D9%86-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A7-%D9%85%D8%B9-%D8%AD%D8%B1%D8%A8-%D8%A5%D9%8A%D8%B1%D8%A7%D9%86))

The violence affecting the Alawite community in early 2026 appears to be characterised by sporadic, low-casualty incidents instead of a large-scale escalation, but recent developments could suggest an increase in the risk of sectarian tensions. These tensions may have risen following reports of a coordinated plot by remnants of the former Al Assad regime to support Alawite armed groups in launching an insurgency against the Government. Leaked audio recordings implicate Brigadier General Suheil Al Hassan and exiled billionaire Rami Makhlouf, operating from Moscow, in attempts to establish weapons caches and command centres in coastal towns of Lattakia governorate with significant Alawite populations. In response, the Government filed an official request for the repatriation of more than 200 senior officers from the previous regime believed to be hiding in Lebanon. Security operations targeting suspected Al Assad loyalists have resulted in multiple arrests of Alawites accused of "threatening the region's stability and pledging loyalty to the former regime". In one January raid, 25 people were arrested, of whom 17 were subsequently released. By 26 January, the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights had documented 18 deaths in retaliatory killings in 2026, including 11 in Homs governorate. These arrests and violence risk deepening Alawite communities' sense of collective punishment and marginalisation, while the discovery of the plot may fuel existing anger towards the Alawite community, potentially leading to further cycles of violence. ([CA-SYR 02/2026](https://ca-syr.org/periodical/january-2026-monthly-report), [SOHR 26/01/2026](https://www.syriahr.com/en/376912/), [Reuters 05/12/2025](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/assads-exiled-spy-chief-billionaire-cousin-plot-syrian-uprisings-russia-2025-12-05/))

Sectarian tensions continue to be reported in Syria. On 23 November 2025, an imam and his wife were killed in Homs governorate. People found sectarian slogans at the crime scene. The crime sparked widespread anger among members of the tribe which the imam belongs to, who then attacked neighbourhoods inhabited by Alawite Syrians in Al Muhajireen and Al Baseel districts of Homs. They fired shots into the air and at homes and shops, as well as set fire to several cars, injuring two people, before security forces arrived in the area to restore order and impose a curfew from 17:00–5:00. Until 24 November, no reports indicated a displacement from Homs resulting from these escalations. ([Al-Quds Al-Arabi 23/11/2025](https://www.alquds.co.uk/%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A7-%D8%AA%D9%88%D8%AA%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%AD%D9%85%D8%B5-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%AE%D9%84%D9%81%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%AC%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%85%D8%A9-%D9%82%D8%AA%D9%84/), [TNA 24/11/2025](https://www.newarab.com/news/syria-extends-curfew-homs-after-murder-sectarian-violence))

Sectarian violence has surged in western Syria and mixed urban zones, with localised attacks by cells affiliated with the Military Council for the Liberation of Syria, contributing to continued instability. In August 2025, retaliatory raids targeting Alawite villages in Rural Hama and Homs governorates caused thousands of Alawite families to flee, marking a new wave of internal displacement explicitly linked to sectarian tensions. Aid organisations report challenges in reaching displaced Alawite populations owing to increased security blockages and partial exclusion in government-controlled areas. Property-based evictions have continued, with many Alawite households forcibly removed in Damascus and Homs governorates since July under the revived properties committee, reigniting grievances and heightening economic marginalisation. Investigations into March’s killings remain stalled, fuelling distrust and perceptions of impunity, with rights groups warning of near-term risk of intensified reprisals. ([SCR 29/08/2025](https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/monthly-forecast/2025-09/syria-83.php), [UN 14/08/2025](https://news.un.org/en/story/2025/08/1165649), [Syria Direct 10/09/2025](https://syriadirect.org/evictions-in-alawite-slums-of-al-somoriyeh-reignite-historic-property-disputes/), [Reuters 13/09/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/how-syrian-forces-emptied-alawite-suburb-x-means-stay-o-means-go-2025-09-12/), [Euronews 02/09/2025](https://www.euronews.com/2025/09/02/alawites-flee-homes-in-damascus-suburb-after-threats-from-armed-group))

On 20 July 2025, Syrian President Ahmed Al Sharaa received from the National Fact-Finding and Investigation Committee the long-awaited final report on the violence in Syria's coastal region in March 2025. The report details the violence that occurred after clashes between armed groups aligned with Bashar Al Assad's rule and loyalists from the Alawite minority. The presidency's office announced that the findings will be carefully reviewed to prevent a recurrence of the violence, and the committee was asked to hold a press conference to ensure transparency and protect evidence. The committee conducted four months of investigations, including interviews with witnesses and site visits.
The actions that the transitional Government will take to hold involved officials, military generals, and armed groups accountable for the March massacres are key to contain further tensions and clashes. ([TNA 20/07/2025](https://www.newarab.com/news/syria-president-receives-report-march-sectarian-violence))

rationaleUpdates.text: This risk has largely materialised. Until 24 November 2025, about 187,000 people remained displaced owing to clashes and insecurity in Al Sweida governorate. Since the clashes broke out between Druze and Bedouin communities in July, government forces have been struggling to restore safety and security, indicating their weak control over armed groups. The people affected continue to face disruptions in services, such as shortages in health supplies, intermittent constraints in access, and deteriorating electricity and telecommunications services. High protection needs are also reported as a result of localised clashes, movement restrictions, and sporadic security incidents, including explosive ordnance-related casualties. Needs for food continue to be high, driven by shortages of bread given the limited supplies entering the governorate, resulting in the closure of bakeries. Humanitarian aid trucks can enter the governorate, but tensions and sporadic violence along key routes, such as the Damascus–Al Sweida route, often restrict access. These also limit civilian movement and access to essential services. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [IMC 19/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/sweida-emergency-response-situation-report-u6-november-19-2025))

Clashes escalated between Druze and Bedouin militias between 11–20 July, triggered by the reported robbery and assault of a Druze merchant by Bedouin gunmen on the Damascus-Al Sweida highway on 11 July. Israeli forces conducted airstrikes on Syrian security forces that attempted to enter Al Sweida, with the pretext to neutralize threats against the Druze community and keep southern Syria a demilitarised area. A ceasefire was reached on 20 July after violent clashes that led to the killing of at least 1,300 people, including civilians and armed men from both sides and Syrian security forces.  These clashes exacerbated sectarian tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government and among the Druze community itself, as Al Hijri seeks collaboration with Israeli forces. 
As of 21 July, the clashes displaced at least 93,000 people, mostly within Al Sweida, others went to Dar’a and Rural Damascus governorates. IDPs are staying with relatives or public building such as schools and mosques, and they need shelter, ready to eat meals, clean water, and medical care. Power outages, unstable internet and mobile connection, and severe shortage in water supply and medical services are reported in Al Sweida. ([UNHCR 21/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/fba9ec77-7b57-4aa0-849e-4a43472838a4/EXTERNAL%20%233%20Flash%20update%20on%20the%20situation%20in%20Sweida%2021%20July%202025.pdf), [SARI Global 23/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/f98c4560-6fe4-4bea-b6a1-508fa7c53803/SWEIDA%E2%80%99S%20CEASEFIRE%2C%20A%20TENUOUS%20CALM%20AMID%20TENSIONS.pdf))

triggers.title: Weak control over Sunni armed groups
Fractured security landscape

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has further deteriorated as Israeli military expansion in southern Syria continues to drive local tensions, with protests against Israel’s advances and continued presence in Syrian territory reported in southern governorates in June 2026. The demonstrations in As Sweida and surrounding areas reflected the growing opposition of communities to Israeli military activity and concerns over sovereignty, despite Israel’s stated objective of preventing threats from armed groups and protecting Druze communities. The protests indicate that Israeli expansion risks increasing local resentment and could contribute to further instability, particularly in Druze-majority areas, where Israel has sought to position itself as a security party. ([SANA 19/06/2026](https://sana.sy/en/photos/2324228/), [Arab News 30/06/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2649041/middle-east), [AJ 29/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/29/new-israeli-assault-in-southern-syria-forces-families-to-flee-their-homes))

The risk has deteriorated. Israeli incursions in April 2026 reflected a pattern of near-daily raids, arrests, and movement restrictions in southern Syria. On 11 April, Israeli forces conducted incursions into the towns of Kudna in Quneitra governorate and Wadi Al Raqad and Hamata in Daraa, by the Yarmouk Basin, arresting at least three civilians during house raids. The operations followed artillery shelling on 10 April targeting Jamlah town, damaging agricultural land. Around 12 military vehicles were involved in at least one incursion. Later in the month, protests erupted in southern Syria and Damascus, organised by families of Syrians detained by Israeli forces, indicating a deterioration in the risk given the increase in Israeli raids. ([AJ 11/04/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/4/11/%D9%82%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%AA%D8%AA%D9%88%D8%BA%D9%84-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%AF%D8%B1%D8%B9%D8%A7), [EB 27/04/2026](https://english.enabbaladi.net/archives/2026/04/damascus-protesters-urge-action-on-syrians-held-by-israel/))

The risk continues to be valid but stable. On 28 March 2026, Israeli forces arrested a Syrian man and a child in southern Quneitra and conducted a ground incursion into Jbata Al Khashab town in the north, including house raids and searches. These incidents are part of a pattern of near-daily incursions in southern Syria involving the arrest of civilians, including herders and children. The continuation of these operations indicates a normalisation of Israeli ground activity inside Syrian territory, contributing to persistent insecurity in border communities. Recurrent raids, checkpoints, and arrests are likely to increase protection risks, restrict civilian movement and livelihoods, and further constrain the Syrian Government’s capacity to restore security, attract investment, and improve economic conditions in the south. ([AJ 01/03/2026](https://www.aljazeera.net/news/2026/3/1/%D8%A5%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84-%D8%AA%D8%AD%D8%B4%D8%AF-100-%D8%A3%D9%84%D9%81-%D9%85%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%AA%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%B7-%D9%88%D8%AA%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%86))

Tensions in southern Syria have intensified since December 2025, driven by the Government's strategic shift towards consolidating control following its northeast offensive and Israel's continued military incursions.
A US-brokered agreement in January 2026 established joint Israeli–Syrian intelligence-sharing mechanisms on movements of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant, but negotiations stalled over future control of Mount Hermon, held by Israel since 2024. Israeli forces continued arrests and roadblocks in Quneitra governorate and launched strikes on Hezbollah targets on the Lebanese border post-agreement, demonstrating parallel diplomatic and military strategies. As Sweida Governor Mustafa Al Bakkour launched a ‘comprehensive settlement initiative’ to bring the governorate under state control, but Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, a prominent Druze spiritual leader, rejected this outright, demanding an independent Druze region with Israel as security guarantor. The Government has responded by providing services to undermine separatist narratives while strengthening its security posture. The collapse of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) represents a setback to Israel's reported strategy of fragmenting Syria into smaller constituent regions, potentially increasing Israeli reliance on Druze militias.
Key escalation risks are apparent. The Government's offensive against the SDF in the northeast may embolden further pursuit of a unitary Syrian state. Syrian forces recognise that Israeli intervention on behalf of Druze communities is highly probable, unlike US restraint during the SDF offensive. While the likeliest scenario is the current status quo, any southern escalation raises the potential for a protracted, multiparty conflict with substantially higher civilian displacement, humanitarian needs, and potential for prolonged instability compared to the rapid northeast campaign. Despite its relatively swift conclusion, the northeast offensive displaced 190,000 people at peak displacement; a protracted southern campaign could have deeper ramifications for large populations, including in the governorates of Dar'a (1.3 million), As Sweida (480,000 people), Quneitra (111,000), sections of Hama, and southern Rural Damascus.
([CA-SYR 02/2026](https://ca-syr.org/periodical/january-2026-monthly-report), [The National 07/02/2026](https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2026/02/08/syrias-fragile-unity-faces-a-new-test-in-sweidas-druze-heartland/), [EUAA 02/12/2026](https://www.euaa.europa.eu/publications/country-guidance-syria-3), [The Syrian Observer 15/01/2026](https://syrianobserver.com/foreign-actors/israel-syria-security-agreement-stalls-over-mount-hermon-and-russian-presence.html), [IOM 31/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-emergency-mobility-tracking-situation-report-alepponorth-east-syria-nes-conflict-round-8-29-january-2026))

In November, Israeli forces continued their incursions in southern Syria, specifically in the northern Quneitra governorate countryside. The Israeli army has advanced in civilian farmlands, destroyed hundreds of acres of forests, and uprooted olive trees, further disrupting people’s livelihoods. They have also arrested residents and established military checkpoints. In October, Israeli forces established a barrier preventing farmers from reaching their land and restricting civilian movement. For example, checkpoints and barriers set up by the Israeli army have cut off all communication between Hamidiyeh, one of the largest farming towns in the region, and Khan Arnaba, the economic and administrative centre of Quneitra. This has forcibly displaced dozens of families in Hamidiyeh from their homes, while those who remain depend highly on humanitarian aid. That said, aid is not always available because of humanitarian access restrictions, mainly road closures. ([OCHA 13/11/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-humanitarian-response-southern-syria-situation-report-no-3-11-november-2025), [HRW 17/09/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syria-israel-forcibly-displaces-villagers-occupied-south-enarhe), [Daily Sabah 22/11/2025](https://www.dailysabah.com/world/mid-east/israel-expands-military-raids-into-syrias-southern-countryside), [Le Monde 10/11/2025](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2025/11/10/on-the-syrian-golan-heights-israel-uses-the-same-tools-of-repression-as-in-the-west-bank_6747318_4.html))

Clashes escalated between Druze and Bedouin militias between 11–20 July, triggered by the reported robbery and assault of a Druze merchant by Bedouin gunmen on the Damascus-Al Sweida highway on 11 July. Israeli forces conducted airstrikes on Syrian security forces that attempted to enter Al Sweida, with the pretext to neutralize threats against the Druze community and keep southern Syria a demilitarised area. Under the stated objective of protecting the Druze community, Israel carried out targeted airstrikes against Syrian military positions in Sweida and Damascus, including strategic sites like the Defence Ministry and areas near the presidential palace. These interventions, combined with Israel's reported coordination with the US to permit the deployment of Syrian Internal Security Forces, demonstrate its growing influence over the security dynamics in southern Syria. 
A ceasefire was reached on 20 July after violent clashes that led to the killing of at least 1,300 people, including civilians and armed men from both sides and Syrian security forces.  These clashes exacerbated sectarian tensions between the Druze and the transitional Government and among the Druze community itself, as Al Hijri seeks collaboration with Israeli forces. ([SARI Global 23/07/2025](https://reliefweb.int/attachments/f98c4560-6fe4-4bea-b6a1-508fa7c53803/SWEIDA%E2%80%99S%20CEASEFIRE%2C%20A%20TENUOUS%20CALM%20AMID%20TENSIONS.pdf))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk improved slightly in April 2026 after tensions rose in March with an escalation between Hezbollah and Israel. Because of insecurity at the border, the Syrian transitional Government increased its military presence at Al Masnaa crossing and deployed more forces, establishing at least three new checkpoints and intensifying searches of travellers and vehicles. Tensions in March increased because of artillery shells being fired from Lebanon and landing in western Damascus. On 4 April, the Israeli military announced its intention to strike Al Masnaa crossing, citing Hezbollah's use of it for military purposes and the smuggling of combat equipment and urging residents to evacuate. Lebanese security sources confirmed evacuating the crossing following the Israeli threat. ([TNA 09/03/2026](https://www.newarab.com/analysis/why-tensions-are-rising-syria-lebanon-border), [Al-Monitor 04/04/2026](https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/04/israel-says-will-strike-lebanon-syria-border-crossing))

Border tensions between Syria and Lebanon have stabilized since late 2025, despite one minor clash near Hermel in December, with both governments pursuing cooperative measures amid underlying security concerns. On 5 February, Lebanon and Syria reached a deal to repatriate approximately 300 Syrian inmates from Lebanese prisons, a priority for Damascus since Al Assad's fall and a signal of improving bilateral relations. However, Damascus filed a separate extradition request for over 200 former regime officers allegedly in Lebanon accused of using Lebanese territory to finance Alawite insurgency operations, led by Brigadier General Suheil Al Hassan and billionaire Rami Makhlouf in Moscow. Syrian authorities continue intercepting weapons and drug smuggling attempts, seizing assault rifles, RPG launchers, Iranian Shahed drones, and ammunition in January heading to Hezbollah via border crossings near Tartous and Sarghaya, alongside ongoing Captagon interdiction efforts. Israeli airstrikes on four Syria–Lebanon border crossings used by Hezbollah for arms smuggling in January complicated dynamics. Turkey has facilitated limited communication between Damascus and Hezbollah to defuse tensions, though Hezbollah justifies retaining weapons citing potential Syrian threats.
([CA-SYR 02/2026](https://ca-syr.org/periodical/january-2026-monthly-report), [Al Jazeera 11/02/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/2/11/why-is-the-issue-of-syrian-prisoner-repatriation-from-lebanon-complicated), [Le Monde 01/02/2026](https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/02/01/between-lebanon-and-syria-the-search-for-a-fresh-start-since-assad-s-fall-and-hezbollah-s-collapse_6750025_4.html), [L'Orient Today 14/12/2025](https://today.lorientlejour.com/article/1488404/clashes-between-lebanese-army-and-syrian-general-security-agents-near-hermel.html), [Times of Israel 17/01/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/syria-says-it-foiled-attempt-to-smuggle-rifles-drones-into-lebanon-via-illegal-border-crossing/), [Times of Israel 26/01/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/syrias-new-regime-says-it-stopped-weapons-shipment-heading-to-hezbollah-in-lebanon/))

Tensions on the Syria–Lebanon borders continue to be reported, contributing to the increased likelihood of clashes. On 15 November, residents of Jrajir town in Qalamoun region (of Syria) protested at the informal Zamrani border crossing after the Lebanese army began establishing military points on their privately owned agricultural lands, which contain over 100,000 fruit trees (mainly cherries and apples). These lands have been inaccessible to farmers since 2017, when Syrian government forces and Hezbollah took control of the Qalamoun Mountains. On 13 November, foreign fighters from the Syrian army were redeployed from the Harem area in Idleb governorate to Al Qusayr, near the Syria–Lebanon border, alongside the movement of heavy military equipment and armoured units. At the same time, forces linked to the Ministry of Defense of the Syrian Transitional Government attempted to advance into Lebanese territory in Wadi Al Thalajat in Ras Al Ma‘ara, an area without Lebanese army presence. These deployments took place at the same time as clashes between Syrian army units and cells of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria positioned opposite the Lebanese town of Arsal. ([The Cradle 13/11/2025](https://thecradle.co/articles/exclusive-syria-deploys-foreign-fighters-to-lebanon-border#google_vignette), [SOHR 15/11/2025](https://www.syriahr.com/%D8%A7%D8%AD%D8%AA%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%AC-%D8%B4%D8%B9%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%AC%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%AC%D9%8A%D8%B1-%D8%A8%D8%B1%D9%8A%D9%81-%D8%AF%D9%85%D8%B4%D9%82-%D8%B6%D8%AF-%D8%A5%D9%86%D8%B4%D8%A7/784475/))

In September, media reports indicated that Hezbollah was working to retrieve weapons stored in Syria, including former Syrian army stockpiles and arms held by Iranian-backed militias, to rebuild capabilities weakened by Israeli strikes. Between July–September, the Syrian Government foiled around 13 smuggling attempts from Syria into Lebanon, most involving weapon shipments. Although Syrian authorities say they control over 75% of the Syria–Lebanon border, security gaps remain, mainly along the rugged border areas near Homs governorate, the Syrian Coast, and Qalamoun region, allowing smuggling operations to continue. ([Majjala 04/09/2025](https://www.majalla.com/node/327209/%D8%B3%D9%8A%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%A9/%D8%AD%D8%B2%D8%A8-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%84%D9%87-%D9%8A%D8%B5%D8%B1-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A8-%D8%A3%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%AD%D8%AA%D9%87-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%B2%D9%86%D8%A9-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A7))

The transitional Government continues with efforts to combat the smuggling of drugs and weapons. In July 2025, the Syrian Ministry of Interior confirmed being engaged in a non-publicised security cooperation with Saudi Arabia focused on combating the trafficking of drugs – especially Captagon – and remnants of the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. The collaboration includes intelligence sharing, joint operations, and planned Saudi-led training for Syrian personnel. Both sides have held multiple meetings to deepen cooperation across areas including border control, tackling organised crime, and institutional development, with Saudi officials expressing commitment to supporting Syria’s security and stability. ([Asharq Al-Awsat accessed 23/07/2025](https://aawsat.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AE%D9%84%D9%8A%D8%AC/5185620-%D8%AA%D8%B1%D8%AD%D9%8A%D8%A8-%D8%B9%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A-%D9%88%D8%A5%D8%B3%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%85%D9%8A-%D8%A8%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%B9%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%A7%D8%AF-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%85%D9%8A-%D9%84%D9%80%D8%A5%D8%B9%D9%84%D8%A7%D9%86-%D9%86%D9%8A%D9%88%D9%8A%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%83))

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk of mass breakouts from Al Hol and Al Roj camps nearly materialized during the January 2026 control transfer from Kurdish-led forces to the transitional Government but has since substantially decreased. Riots erupted in Al Hol's Syrian and Iraqi sections, with residents burning a bakery and tents as NGOs and security personnel withdrew, creating temporary security vacuums. However, the International Coalition and CENTCOM have transferred over 4,500 detainees to Iraq, and Al Hol's foreign annex, which previously held 6,200 foreign nationals, is now almost empty. The transitional Government announced plans to permanently close both camps within a year. Foreign governments continue refusing to repatriate their nationals detained for IS links, leaving Iraq to absorb foreign fighters. Separately, 120 ISIS detainees escaped from Al Shaddadi prison in Hasakah governorate on 19 January, with 81 recaptured and 39 remaining at large who could rejoin active ISIS cells. ([Al Jazeera 19/01/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/19/isil-fighters-flee-jail-as-syrian-army-clashes-with-kurdish-led-sdf), [The Guardian 22/01/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jan/22/open-the-gates-riots-fires-and-escape-attempts-as-syrian-army-takes-over-is-camp), [Al-Monitor 11/02/2026](https://www.al-monitor.com/originals/2026/02/syrian-kurdish-officials-say-66-turkish-isis-fighters-transferred-relocation-iraq), [MEE 12/02/2026](https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/syrias-al-hol-camp-emptied-foreigners-sources-say), [Manassa 10/02/2026](https://manassa.news/en/news/30223))

As of November, the risk of unrest and breakout attempts in Al Hol and Al Roj camps continues to be reported. As US funding cuts of at least 117 million dollars have severely weakened security and services in al-Hol and Roj camps, more than 20 humanitarian projects including medical, mental health, and child-protection activities were affected. Children are now more vulnerable to radicalisation, while escape attempts have increased. There are reportedly audio messages from ISIS members circulating urging supporters to launch “individual jihad” operations to help the detainees in the camps, likely creating a major security crisis that could trigger a mass breakout. Since the May deal enabling departures from al-Hol to government-controlled areas, only around 360 Syrians have returned due to political delays, restrictive procedures, and limited aid capacity. ([Shia Waves 27/11/2025](https://shiawaves.com/english/news/islam/syria/137319-warning-over-security-crisis-in-northeast-syrias-isis-detention-camps/), [TNH 12/11/2025](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2025/11/12/despite-promises-returns-notorious-syrian-camp-remain-rare)).

rationaleUpdates.text: The risk has slightly improved because above-average rainfall in February and March 2026 provided some short-term relief to water availability in parts of Syria. However, structural drivers of water scarcity remain in place, including damaged water infrastructure, limited pumping and treatment capacity, and the long-term effects of climate change. At the same time, several flooding events affected Al Hasakah, Ar Raqqa, and Deir ez Zor governorates, impacting an estimated 6,000 people in March. Additional heavy rainfall affected approximately 19,000 people in Aleppo and Idlib governorates. While the rainfall may temporarily improve water availability and soil moisture in some areas, flooding has also damaged crops, agricultural land, and infrastructure, potentially reducing food production and access to food for affected communities.

Water scarcity has intensified since December 2025, with catastrophic agricultural impacts. Wheat production has falled by over 50% compared to pre-war norms, while barley production has dropped by 65% below the five-year average as a result of drought, extreme heat, insecurity, and high input costs. Agricultural drought models indicate over 700,000 hectares in central and northern Syria will face drought between January–March 2026, with Aleppo, Al Hasakeh, Ar Raqqa, Hama, and Idleb governorates worst affected. In early February, flash floods in Idleb and Lattakia killed at least two children and inundated displacement camps. While rainfall is desperately needed, intense storms risk washing away fertile topsoil rather than replenishing reservoirs. During January clashes, residents in Aleppo and Al Hasakeh experienced days without water after authorities took control of Tishreen Dam. The transitional Government's northeast takeover has transferred water management from Kurdish-led authorities to Damascus. Damascus has reaffirmed commitments to share 58% of Euphrates flows with Iraq and announced multilevel water governance reforms, though implementation details remain pending.
([FEWS NET 31/12/2025](https://fews.net/middle-east-and-asia/syria/special-report/december-2025), [IOM 19/12/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-population-mobility-and-baseline-assessment-round-10-november-2025), [TNA 08/02/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/two-killed-others-missing-flash-floods-hit-northwest-syria))

Some of the triggers suggested are materialising as rainfall dropped nationwide, with Damascus receiving only 29% of its annual average compared with 86% in 2024, and Al Sweida and Daraa falling to less than half of 2024 levels. Flooding from intense, uneven rain failed to replenish reservoirs. War damage has left irrigation systems over 500,000 hectares largely nonfunctional. Reduced surface-water flows and groundwater recharge have triggered a nationwide water crisis affecting more than 80% of the population. Over 75% of cultivated crops and grazing areas are impacted, with livestock numbers down by 40% and feed prices are up by 100–300%. Vegetable prices have risen by 20–40% amid reduced production and disrupted road access between areas controlled by different authorities. Across northeast Syria, prolonged drought and delayed rainfall have severely depleted rivers, wells, and soil moisture, threatening rain-fed agriculture in key areas such as Qamishli, Amuda, and Hasakeh. Although no protests or social unrest have been reported because of water scarcity, but some analysts consider climate-driven livelihood collapse as a contributing factor to the July clashes between Druze and Bedouin communities in Al Sweida, in addition to factors such as disputes over land and smuggling routes and state manipulation. Farmers in western rural Al Sweida have lost over 70% of their olive harvest this season because drought, insecurity, and displacement have prevented them from reaching their land, while armed groups have looted crops, dismantled the main Thaala olive press, and cut trees for firewood.([BBC 17/09/2025](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c70x500lkdno), [IFRC 30/08/2025](https://reliefweb.int/report/syrian-arab-republic/syrian-arab-republic-drought-2025-dref-operation-mdrsy017), [Shafaq 23/08/2025](https://shafaq.com/en/Middle-East/Drought-and-war-leave-Syria-struggling-with-water-shortages), [Ultra Syria 17/11/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D9%81%D8%A7%D9%81-%D9%8A%D9%88%D8%A7%D8%B5%D9%84-%D8%AA%D9%87%D8%AF%D9%8A%D8%AF-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%82%D9%85%D8%AD-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%B4%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%84-%D9%88%D8%B4%D8%B1%D9%82-%D8%B3%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%8A%D8%A7-%D9%88%D9%85%D8%B7%D8%B1-%D9%85%D8%AA%D8%A3%D8%AE%D8%B1-%D9%8A%D8%AB%D9%8A%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%84-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%87%D8%B4/%D9%87%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%8A/%D9%85%D8%AC%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%B9-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%82%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%AF), [Ultra Syria 18/11/2025](https://ultrasyria.ultrasawt.com/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B2%D9%8A%D8%AA%D9%88%D9%86-%D9%81%D9%8A-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B3%D9%88%D9%8A%D8%AF%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%A8%D9%8A%D9%86-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AC%D9%81%D8%A7%D9%81-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%86%D8%B2%D9%88%D8%AD-%D9%85%D9%88%D8%B3%D9%85-%D8%B6%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%B9-%D9%88%D9%85%D8%AD%D8%A7%D8%B5%D9%8A%D9%84-%D9%85%D9%86%D9%87%D9%88%D8%A8%D8%A9/%D8%B9%D9%85%D8%B1%D9%88-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AD%D9%8A%D8%AB%D8%A7%D9%88%D9%8A/%D9%85%D8%AC%D8%AA%D9%85%D8%B9-%D9%88%D8%A7%D9%82%D8%AA%D8%B5%D8%A7%D8%AF), [AJ 02/09/2025](https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2025/9/2/the-druze-bedouin-clashes-in-syria-were-not-a-sectarian-conflict)).
